title: Beyond Browsing: API-Based Web Agents
venue: Findings of ACL 2025 (ACL Anthology 2025.findings-acl.577); arXiv v1 Oct 2024, v3 Jun 2025
core_idea: Gives WebArena agents API access (official docs/OpenAPI, LLM-written READMEs, or hand-added endpoints) and compares a browsing-only agent, an API-only agent and a Hybrid agent that interleaves API calls and browsing within a task. Large API sets (>100 endpoints) are handled with a two-stage get_api_documentation retrieval tool rather than stuffing all docs in the prompt.
headline_results: WebArena (812 tasks), GPT-4o backbone for all agents, Table 2 average success: Browsing 14.8%, API-Based 29.2%, Hybrid 38.9% ('more than 24.0% absolute improvement over web browsing alone'; 'SOTA among task-agnostic agents'). Per-site Hybrid: Gitlab 44.4, Map 45.9, Shopping 25.7, Admin 41.2, Reddit 51.9, Multi 16.7. API-only beats browsing on Gitlab (43.9 vs 12.8) but not Admin (20.3 vs 22.0) or Multi (8.3 vs 10.4). Table 7: avg steps 8.4/7.8/8.5; avg cost per task ~$0.1 browsing vs ~$1.2 API vs ~$1.4 Hybrid (API docs inflate prompts; Gitlab exposes 988 APIs). v1 reported Hybrid 35.8%; v3 reports 38.9%.
implement_or_borrow: Directly the template for the API agent: expose named, parameterised server operations with OpenAPI-style docs; if the catalogue exceeds ~100 ops, add a get_api_documentation(op) retrieval tool (two-stage: list names/one-line descriptions, then fetch full schema) so a 14B/32B context is not swamped. Run the same task set in API-only, VACP-only and hybrid modes to reproduce their 3-way comparison on our app.
risks: All numbers are GPT-4o only; no open-model results. API docs blew cost up ~12x vs browsing (prompt length) - matters for local context windows. Some APIs were hand-added by authors, so API coverage was curated. Hybrid gains come mostly from sites where API coverage is partial.
hybrid_evidence: Yes, strongest web evidence: Hybrid 38.9% vs API-only 29.2% vs browsing 14.8% on WebArena (GPT-4o); Hybrid >= both on every site.
small_model_evidence: None in paper (GPT-4o only). The Tool Illusion (2604.03465) re-ran these human-crafted APIs with GPT-5-nano: 10.1 -> 22.5 on WebArena.

title: Internal APIs Are All You Need: Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures
core_idea: Unbrowse passively learns a site's first-party internal ('shadow') API routes from real browser network traffic (filtering by content-type, URL pattern, method, response shape) and serves them from a shared route graph so later agents call endpoints directly. A three-path executor uses local cache, then shared graph, then browser fallback with re-learning; the paper also proposes x402 micropayment tiers.
headline_results: Single-host live-web benchmark, 94 domains, info-retrieval tasks modelled on WebArena: warmed cached execution mean 950 ms vs 3,404 ms Playwright (3.6x mean speedup, 5.4x median per-domain), median 630 ms vs 3,402 ms; 18 domains under 100 ms; best 30x (79 vs 2,289 ms). Cold start on 20 unseen domains: median 8,200 ms, mean 12,400 ms; skill publish success 18/20. WAF-protected sites (9/94) median speedup 2.1x vs 6.8x unprotected.
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the three-path executor pattern for the VACP agent: prefer a cached/direct server operation, fall back to the in-page bridge, fall back last to Playwright; log which path was used per step as a latency KPI. Optionally record the app's own XHR traffic during demo flows to auto-generate/validate the operation catalogue. Skip the payment model.
risks: Self-reported by authors affiliated with Unbrowse AI; single host in Singapore; latency only, no task-success/accuracy metric (tasks Playwright could not match were excluded); n=20 cold start; auth/OAuth and anti-bot limitations; legal/ToS issues with shadow APIs on third-party sites (not an issue for our own app).
hybrid_evidence: Latency only: cached API path 3.6x mean / 5.4x median faster than Playwright; browser kept as fallback. No accuracy comparison.

title: Terminal Agents Suffice for Enterprise Automation
core_idea: Compares MCP tool-use agents, Playwright-MCP web agents and a terminal+filesystem coding agent (StarShell) that calls platform REST APIs directly, on 729 enterprise tasks across ServiceNow, GitLab and ERPNext. Argues simple programmatic interfaces plus strong models beat heavier architectures; also tests a terminal+browser hybrid, documentation and reusable 'skills' files.
code_url: none found (paper: 'will be released upon acceptance'; only third-party MCP servers linked)
implement_or_borrow: Strongest evidence for our API agent design and for giving a 27-32B model a code/compose capability: let the planner chain parameterised operations in a small sandboxed Python step (no free SQL) for multi-step analysis. Borrow the 'skills' idea: a concise task-oriented markdown of how to answer common analytics intents with our ops (they found human-oriented reference docs can mislead). ERPNext tasks are a close analogue for our orders/inventory/purchasing/invoices data.
risks: Main results are frontier closed models; terminal agent gets near-unrestricted API/code access (we forbid free SQL - guardrails needed). Terminal fails where state lives only in UI (impersonation 0%, dashboard chart values must be reconstructed, drag-and-drop flow editing). Web beat terminal on GitLab for every model. No code released.
hybrid_evidence: Hybrid terminal+browser: Opus 81.4% vs web 79.9% vs terminal 78.7% (small gain); Sonnet 72.0% vs 72.2%/72.7% (no gain) at higher cost ($1.94 vs $0.56).
small_model_evidence: Qwen-3.6-27B: terminal 54.5% vs MCP tool-use 31.9% vs web 34.8% overall; ERPNext terminal 56.0%, tool-use 48.3%, web 34.3%. Gemma-4-31B terminal 46.1%. Open models lose least vs frontier in tool-use mode (-5.2 pp Qwen) and most in web mode (-34.1 pp).

title: Web Agents Should Use Typed Actions Instead of Click-Based Browsing
venue: ICML 2026 Position Paper Track (per arXiv comments)
core_idea: Position paper proposing 'web verbs': typed, documented functions with structured inputs/outputs, backed by a server-side Web API or a maintained client-side (Playwright) workflow, carrying preconditions, postconditions, policy tags and logging hooks. Agents synthesise short programs over verbs with explicit control and data flow, giving checkable traces instead of brittle click sequences.
headline_results: No quantitative benchmark of its own. Case studies (Anchorage travel planning; $1,000 seven-category furniture shopping) where a browser agent answered a different question or used a greedy plan, while verb programs (nested loops/enumeration) were correct. Prototype covers 'more than ten websites' and 'over one hundred distinct complex tasks', which it says all completed successfully (no rates/latency reported).
licence: none detected (GitHub API license=null; no LICENSE file found on main)
implement_or_borrow: Use as the schema for both the API ops and window.__vacp.execute capabilities: each verb gets JSON-schema inputs/outputs, preconditions (e.g., page loaded, filter valid), postconditions checked after execution (getState matches requested filter/date/sort -> UI-state correctness KPI), a policy tag (read-only vs state-changing -> confirmation guardrail) and a log hook (faithfulness trace). Let the model emit a short verb program for comparisons (period A vs B) instead of step-by-step clicks.
risks: Position paper: evidence is anecdotal case studies, no success rates; requires someone to author/maintain verbs (fine for our own app).
hybrid_evidence: Verbs can wrap browser workflows; agent may 'fall back to low-level interaction primitives when needed' - argued, not measured.
small_model_evidence: None.

title: AXIS: Efficient Human-Agent-Computer Interaction with API-First LLM-Based Agents
core_idea: An API-first agent framework that calls application APIs and uses UI actions only when no related API exists. An Explorer agent explores the app and a Translator agent (with RAG over app docs and a skill library) converts UI action sequences into new APIs.
headline_results: Abstract: on Microsoft Word, reduces task completion time by 65%-70% and cognitive workload by 38%-53% while maintaining accuracy of 97%-98% compared to humans. Feasibility study (50 Word tasks) vs UFO UI agent: mean time 29.9 s vs 59.5 s, success 84.0% vs 52.0%, cost $0.2 vs $0.4/task. User study (20 participants, L1/L2): success 98.3%/95.0% vs UI agent 75.0%/45.0%.
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the API-first-with-UI-fallback policy for the VACP agent: planner first checks getCapabilities for a direct op, only falls back to UI-level execute steps when none matches. The Explorer->Translator loop (record a successful UI sequence, promote it to a named op) is a stretch goal.
risks: Single app (Word), GPT-4o/GPT-4 backbone (paper inconsistent), small user study; no open-model results; no code.
hybrid_evidence: API-first with UI fallback vs UI-only agent: 84.0% vs 52.0% success and roughly half the time on 50 Word tasks.

title: SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills
core_idea: An agent explores a new website, proposes skills, practises them, and distils successful trajectories into reusable Python 'APIs' (Playwright functions with docstrings and preconditions) that are unit-tested and added to a growing library. Libraries synthesised by strong agents transfer to weaker agents.
headline_results: Abstract: relative success-rate improvements of 31.8% (WebArena) and 39.8% (real-world sites); APIs from strong agents give weaker agents improvements of up to 54.3% on WebArena. Full text Table 1: GPT-4o WebArena avg 22.6 -> 29.8; GPT-4o-mini 9.2 -> 14.1. Table 2 (Online-Mind2Web, 4 sites, 57 tasks): 40.2 -> 56.2. Paper text is internally inconsistent (also states 39.8% relative on WebArena).
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the skill-honing loop offline: use the 32B model during setup to propose/test composite operations (e.g., 'monthly revenue by region with filter X') against our app, keep only those that pass a unit test, and expose them as named ops for the 14B runtime model (strong-to-weak transfer).
risks: 'APIs' are Playwright UI macros, not server endpoints; GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini only; Tool Illusion (2604.03465) found SkillWeaver tools give small or negative gains for stronger backbones (e.g., GPT-5 39.2 -> 37.4).
small_model_evidence: Weak-model transfer only with GPT-4o-mini (9.2 -> 14.1 WebArena); no open models.

title: WALT: Web Agents that Learn Tools
venue: ICLR 2026 (per ICLR proceedings listing seen in search)
core_idea: Reverse-engineers functionality already built into websites (search, filter, sort, post, create/edit/delete) into validated, deterministic tools so agents call search(query) instead of clicking. Discovery agent demonstrates candidate tools; a construction agent turns traces into scripts (with URL-parameter promotion where possible) and validates them end to end.
headline_results: VisualWebArena 52.9% (vs SGV 50.2%; human 88.7%); WebArena 50.1% (vs ASI 40.4%, Hybrid Agent 38.9%, AWM 35.5%, SkillWeaver 29.8%; human 78.2%). '1.3-1.4x fewer steps on average'. Classifieds ablation: GPT-5-mini 57.5% / 8.9 steps without tools vs 61.5% / 6.5 steps with tools; human-demonstrated tools 66.0%. Backbones GPT-5 (planner) + GPT-5-mini (executor).
implement_or_borrow: Directly mirrors our filter/sort/date-range needs: model each page's UI state as URL/deep-link parameters and expose set_filters/set_sort/set_date_range as deterministic tools (URL-parameter promotion), validated by replay tests. Keep the tool set small (~8 per site in WALT) - easier for 14B tool calling.
risks: Closed GPT-5-family backbones only; Tool Illusion re-run found WALT tools give little gain for strong models (GPT-5 52.9 -> 50.9) but help weaker ones (GPT-5-nano 24.4 -> 28.6). Tools are UI scripts with cached selectors, brittle to layout change.
hybrid_evidence: Tools + browser actions beat prior hybrid/API agents on WebArena (50.1 vs 38.9 Hybrid Agent), but with stronger backbones, so not a controlled comparison.

title: The Tool Illusion: Rethinking Tool Use in Web Agents
core_idea: Controlled re-evaluation of tool use for web agents across tool sources (human-crafted REST APIs from Beyond Browsing, SkillWeaver, WALT), backbones and benchmarks (WebArena, VisualWebArena). Finds synthesised tools help mainly when the tool user is weaker than the synthesiser, and that tool use has a hidden token/step cost.
headline_results: WebArena avg SR without -> with tools: human-crafted APIs (Hybrid-Agent, ~437 tools/site): GPT-5 36.5 -> 49.9, GPT-5-mini 19.3 -> 38.9, GPT-5-nano 10.1 -> 22.5, Grok-4.1-R 26.2 -> 42.7, Mistral-L-3.1 16.6 -> 31.2. WALT (~8 tools/site): GPT-5 52.9 -> 50.9, GPT-5-nano 24.4 -> 28.6. SkillWeaver (~88 tools/site): GPT-5 39.2 -> 37.4, GPT-5-nano 11.0 -> 13.1. API tools composed more: 52% of Hybrid-Agent tasks used >=2 tools (41.2% success) vs 18% WALT, 25% SkillWeaver. Findings: 'More comprehensive tools are not necessarily better'; 'Less comprehensive tools can still be highly effective, as long as they compose well'.
code_url: none found for the study (baseline repos: yueqis/API-Based-Agent, SalesforceAIResearch/WALT, OSU-NLP-Group/SkillWeaver)
implement_or_borrow: Design rule for our op catalogue: human-authored, composable, deterministic ops gave the biggest and most consistent gains across all backbones, including weak ones - so hand-write ~20-40 ops covering common intents rather than auto-synthesising hundreds. Keep grounding/judgement in the agent; measure token and step overhead per tool-library size as part of latency KPI.
risks: No open-weight models (closest: GPT-5-nano, Mistral-Large-3.1). Numbers read from the full-text HTML table via summariser; per-framework 'without tools' baselines differ because each framework has its own harness.
hybrid_evidence: Human-crafted API tools added to a browser agent raise WebArena SR by 12.7-19.6 pp across five backbones (e.g., GPT-5-mini 19.3 -> 38.9); synthesised UI-macro tools give inconsistent gains.
small_model_evidence: Weak backbones benefit most: GPT-5-nano 10.1 -> 22.5 with human APIs. No Qwen/Llama/DeepSeek tested.

title: UFO2: The Desktop AgentOS
core_idea: Multi-agent Windows AgentOS: a HostAgent decomposes tasks and per-application AppAgents act through a unified GUI-API action layer (native app APIs plus UI Automation/vision control detection). Speculative multi-action planning cuts per-step LLM calls; a picture-in-picture virtual desktop isolates execution.
headline_results: Windows Agent Arena / OSWorld-W SR: UFO2 (GPT-4o) 27.9% / 28.6%, UFO2 (o1) 30.5% / 32.7%, vs Operator 20.8% / 14.3% and UFO 19.5% / 12.2%. GUI-only vs GUI+API ablation: GPT-4o 16.3% -> 22.4% (avg steps 13.8 -> 12.9); o1 16.3% -> 24.5% (steps 16.0 -> 6.6). Speculative multi-action lowers 'inference cost by up to 51.5% without compromising reliability' (e.g., WAA GPT-4o steps 10.00 -> 8.78, SR unchanged 23.4%).
implement_or_borrow: Borrow (a) the unified action layer: one action schema whose executor routes to API op or UI bridge, and (b) speculative multi-action: let the model emit several independent UI-state actions (set filter + date + sort) in one turn, executed in sequence with a getState check between - cuts LLM round-trips and latency for 14B/32B models.
risks: Desktop/Windows, GPT-4o/o1 backbones; no open-model results; large codebase not directly reusable for a web app.
hybrid_evidence: Controlled ablation: adding native API actions to GUI raises SR by 6.1 pp (GPT-4o) and 8.2 pp (o1) on OSWorld-W, with o1 steps 16.0 -> 6.6.

title: CoAct-1: Computer-using Multi-Agent System with Coding Actions
core_idea: An Orchestrator delegates each subtask either to a GUI Operator (computer-use model) or a Programmer agent that writes and runs Python/Bash, letting the system bypass long GUI sequences for data processing and file work while keeping visual interaction when needed.
headline_results: OSWorld: 60.76% at 150 steps (new SOTA claimed); 59.93% at 100 steps vs Agent S2.5 w/ o3 55.98%, GTA-1-7B w/ o3 53.07%, OpenAI CUA 4o 31.38%; at 15 steps 39.81% (below Jedi-7B 42.37%). Avg 10.15 steps vs 15 for leading GUI agents. Ablation: Programmer-only 35.73%, GUI-Operator-only 50.68%, full hybrid 60.76%. Models: o3 orchestrator, o4-mini programmer, computer-use-preview GUI operator.
implement_or_borrow: Orchestrator pattern for the hybrid build: planner routes each sub-goal to either the API/analysis worker (ops + sandboxed pandas over op results) or the VACP UI worker (navigate/set state so the user sees the evidence). Use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B as orchestrator/analyst, Qwen2.5-14B as the fast tool-calling executor.
risks: All closed OpenAI models; desktop benchmark; code licence is non-commercial (CC-BY-NC-4.0) - fine for hackathon reference but do not copy code into a commercial product.
hybrid_evidence: Clean ablation: hybrid 60.76% vs coding-only 35.73% vs GUI-only 50.68% on OSWorld (150-step budget), with fewer steps.

title: UltraCUA: A Foundation Model for Computer Use Agents with Hybrid Action
core_idea: Trains 7B and 32B computer-use models whose action space mixes GUI primitives with high-level programmatic tool calls, using 881 tools mined from docs, open-source agents and coding-agent trajectories, 17,000+ synthetic verifiable tasks, SFT then online RL.
headline_results: Abstract: 22% relative improvement on OSWorld while executing 11% faster on average; WindowsAgentArena 21.7%. Full text: UltraCUA-7B-RL 28.9% (15 steps) / 30.2% (50) vs base UI-TARS-1.5-7B 23.4/26.1 (reproduced); UltraCUA-32B-RL 41.0 / 43.7 vs base OpenCUA-32B 33.3 / 35.1 (reproduced). Ablation (Table 5): UltraCUA-7B-SFT GUI-only 25.1% (9.24 steps) vs hybrid 27.0% (8.46 steps); GTA1-7B + o3 44.0% -> 48.2% (15.53 -> 13.22 steps). RL cut tool-related failures 46% (122 -> 66).
code_url: none found (no official repo located; third-party raimondasl/ultracua is not official)
implement_or_borrow: Evidence that 7B-32B models can learn GUI-vs-tool selection, but training is out of scope for 48h. Borrow the tool-mining recipe (turn app docs/shortcuts and successful scripts into parameterised functions with unit tests) and the per-domain tool-call counting metric.
risks: Requires SFT+RL on custom data; base models are vision CUA models (UI-TARS, OpenCUA) not our text LLMs; no released weights found.
hybrid_evidence: Hybrid vs GUI-only ablation: +1.9 pp (7B-SFT, 25.1 -> 27.0) and +4.2 pp (GTA1-7B + o3, 44.0 -> 48.2) on OSWorld with fewer steps.
small_model_evidence: 7B: 28.9% OSWorld (15 steps); 32B: 41.0% (15) / 43.7% (50), both trained for hybrid action. 7B makes 0-20 tool calls per domain vs 20-40 for 32B - smaller model uses tools less.

title: MCPWorld: A Unified Benchmarking Testbed for API, GUI, and Hybrid Computer Use Agents
core_idea: Benchmark of 201 tasks on 'white-box' open-source apps, extended with MCP servers, evaluating GUI-only, API(MCP)-only and hybrid agents. Task completion is verified by instrumenting app internals rather than matching UI state.
headline_results: Claude 3.7 Sonnet (computer-use-demo framework), overall SR: GUI-only 70.65%, MCP-only 53.23%, Hybrid 75.12% (abstract: 75.12%). By difficulty: Easy 90.41/63.01/90.41; Medium 72.29/51.81/74.70; Hard (10+ GUI steps) 35.56/40.00/51.11. Removing the Bash tool drops Hybrid 75.12% -> 65.50%.
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the evaluation idea: verify task completion via app-internal state (our window.__vacp.getState and server logs) rather than screenshots, and report results split by step-difficulty buckets for API-only / VACP-only / hybrid modes.
risks: Single closed backbone; desktop apps; API-only weaker because MCP coverage was partial - result depends on coverage.
hybrid_evidence: Hybrid 75.12% vs GUI-only 70.65% vs MCP-only 53.23%; gain concentrated on hard tasks (51.11% vs 35.56% GUI-only).

title: OSWorld-MCP: Benchmarking MCP Tool Invocation In Computer-Use Agents
venue: ICLR 2026 (per ICLR virtual poster listing seen in search; not stated in paper)
core_idea: Extends OSWorld with 158 validated MCP tools across 7 apps (including 25 distractor tools) so agents may choose GUI actions or tool calls at each step. Measures accuracy, Tool Invocation Rate (TIR) and average completion steps.
headline_results: Abstract (v1): MCP tools improve SR from 8.3% to 20.4% for o3 at 15 steps and 40.1% to 43.3% for Claude 4 Sonnet at 50 steps; strongest TIR only 36.3%. Open model rows: Qwen2.5-VL-72B 11.4 -> 15.8 (15 steps, TIR 13.1) and 13.9 -> 14.8 (50 steps, TIR 10.9); Qwen3-VL-Plus 25.4 -> 31.3 (15) and 33.8 -> 39.1 (50). Agent-S2.5 47.1 -> 49.5 (50 steps). Search summaries report the ICLR version changes these (o3 8.3 -> 17.6; Sonnet 38.9 -> 45.0; TIR 33.3%) - not verified from paper.
implement_or_borrow: Adopt TIR and distractor tools in our eval: include near-miss ops in the catalogue and measure whether the agent calls the right op vs hallucinated/wrong ones (action-hallucination KPI) and how often it falls back to UI when an op exists.
risks: Numbers differ between arXiv versions; models under-use tools; desktop setting.
hybrid_evidence: GUI+MCP beats GUI-only for every model listed (e.g., o3 8.3 -> 20.4 at 15 steps), yet TIR <= 36.3%.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-VL-72B gains only +4.4 pp (15 steps) / +0.9 pp (50 steps) with TIR ~11-13% - weaker open models largely ignore available tools.

title: Screenshots or Tools? Eliciting Tool Use and Managing Multimodal Context in Hybrid GUI-MCP Computer-Use Agents
core_idea: Under one GUI-MCP harness on OSWorld-MCP (309 tasks), shows that adding the same MCP tools helps a reasoning 8B model but hurts a non-reasoning 8B model, because of tool-decision failures (ignoring, misnaming, falsely terminating). Probes the 'adoption gap' with multi-turn RL and compresses context by dropping screenshots made redundant by successful tool calls.
headline_results: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking: 30.5% GUI-only -> 34.5% GUI+MCP (+4.0pp); Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct: 25.4% -> 19.5% (-5.9pp) (5 runs each, both beyond 2 SE). Instruct produced 97 hallucinated tool names (Thinking 0); false-success 33.0% (102/309) vs 21.7% (67/309). Thinking calls a tool on 55/309 tasks (23.9% of tool-reachable). Dense tool bonus RL raises spreadsheet adoption 0.03 -> 0.33 but held-out accuracy does not follow. Compressed agent 37.8% vs 33.0% at 53% of input cost.
implement_or_borrow: Directly relevant to our model choice: expect a non-reasoning model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) to misname tools and falsely declare success. Mitigate with constrained decoding/enum-validated tool names (vLLM guided JSON), a hard tool-name allowlist with retry, and a postcondition check before 'done'. Borrow context compression: after a successful op/bridge call, drop the stale state snapshot from history.
risks: Vision CUA setting with 8B VL models; RL results do not transfer to accuracy; one benchmark.
hybrid_evidence: Hybrid helps only if the policy chooses tools well: +4.0pp for reasoning 8B, -5.9pp for non-reasoning 8B.
small_model_evidence: Qwen3-VL-8B Thinking vs Instruct: tools +4.0pp vs -5.9pp; Instruct hallucinated 97 tool names and had 33.0% false-success rate - key warning for Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct tool calling.

title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
core_idea: Benchmark of function calling that scores single-turn serial/parallel calls by AST matching (shown to correlate with execution), plus crowd-sourced live prompts, relevance/irrelevance (abstention), stateful multi-turn API suites and agentic tasks (web search, memory, SQL). Compares native FC mode against prompt mode, in which the function schemas go in the system prompt.
headline_results: Table 1 (overall acc): gpt-4o-2024-11-20 (Prompt) 66.4 (top); Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (Prompt) 57.0; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (FC) 55.6, (Prompt) 52.1; Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (Prompt) 50.4; Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (FC) 49.2, (Prompt) 47.8; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (FC) 44.7; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Prompt) 39.6. Prompting models had ~3x more decoding failures than FC models (412.93 vs 182.5 of 4,251 entries), but in the multiple-function category FC models made more incorrect function-call counts (77.5 vs 21). The authors state that top models do well at single-turn but that memory, dynamic decision-making and long-horizon reasoning remain open.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file; GitHub API was rate-limited)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW the eval harness design. Score our agent's operation calls by AST match (op name plus typed args against a gold call) rather than by exact strings. Add an irrelevance split (requests no operation can serve, where the agent must abstain) to measure action hallucination. Add a multi-turn split with missing-param and missing-function cases (the agent must ask for clarification). Run Qwen2.5-14B in both vLLM native tool-calling (hermes parser) and prompt mode, and keep whichever scores higher on our own set.
risks: Public BFCL categories (Java/JS, generic APIs) do not match our domain, so build our own gold set in BFCL format. Scores shift between BFCL versions (v1/v2/v3/v4), so never compare numbers across versions.
hybrid_evidence: Multi-turn 'Miss Func' and 'Miss Param' categories test whether a model notices that a needed function or argument is missing. This maps onto VACP getCapabilities, where an action may be unavailable on the current page.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (FC): overall 55.6; single-turn AST simple 72.8; irrelevance 81.9; relevance 64.7; multi-turn base 29.5; agentic web search 53.0, memory 4.0, SQL 45.0. Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (FC): overall 49.2; AST simple 69.7; irrelevance 77.7; relevance 55.6; multi-turn base 19.5 (miss-func 17.0, miss-param 16.5, long-context 10.5); web search 30.0; memory 0.0; SQL 30.0. Separately, the official leaderboard (V4 categories; fetched 2026-10-09; page last updated 2026-04-12; NOT the paper) does not list Qwen2.5 or R1-distill models. There, Qwen3-32B (FC) scores 48.71% overall (non-live AST 88.77, live 82.01, multi-turn 47.87), Qwen3-14B (FC) 41.03% (84.94 / 80.01 / 34.75) and xLAM-2-32b-fc-r (FC) 54.66% (89.60 / 75.50 / 69.50).
arxiv_id_title_check: no arXiv ID (checked via official page)

title: Qwen3 Technical Report
core_idea: Technical report for the Qwen3 dense and MoE models, which offer thinking and non-thinking modes in one model. Its baseline tables give BFCL v3 scores for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B/32B, QwQ-32B and Qwen2.5-7B/14B/32B/72B-Instruct, making it the only verified source of R1-distill BFCL numbers found.
headline_results: BFCL v3 (Tables 13-18). Thinking/reasoning models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 53.5; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B 49.5; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B 49.3; QwQ-32B 66.4; OpenAI-o3-mini (medium) 64.6; Qwen3-32B (thinking) 70.3; Qwen3-14B (thinking) 70.4; Qwen3-8B (thinking) 68.1. Non-thinking: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct 63.4; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct 62.8; Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct 58.7; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 55.8; Qwen3-32B 63.0; Qwen3-14B 61.5; GPT-4o-mini 64.0; Gemma-3-27B-IT 59.1; Phi-4 47.0; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 49.6. Qwen3-235B-A22B: 70.8.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML Tables 13-18 and Sec. 4 eval setup)
licence: not checked (no LICENSE file found at repo root; weights licence not verified)
implement_or_borrow: USE AS EVIDENCE for model choice. On BFCL v3, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (53.5) scores below plain Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (58.7) and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (62.8). So route all tool-call or action selection through Qwen2.5-14B/32B-Instruct, and use R1-distill only for offline analytical narration over data already retrieved. If the team can swap models, Qwen3-14B/32B (thinking ~70) is the strongest local option in this report.
risks: These are vendor-reported numbers. Baselines take the higher of FC and Prompt scores from the leaderboard, or a Prompt-format run by Qwen, so they are not head-to-head with BFCL paper Table 1 (which gives Qwen2.5-14B FC 49.2). BFCL v3 overall weighting also differs from v4.
small_model_evidence: BFCL v3: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 53.5 vs Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct 62.8, and R1-Distill-Qwen-14B 49.5 vs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct 58.7. Distillation from R1 costs about 9 points of tool-calling at both sizes. QwQ-32B 66.4.

title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
core_idea: Pure and multi-stage RL induces long chain-of-thought reasoning, and the resulting traces are distilled into Qwen/Llama dense models (the R1-Distill series). Relevant here only for its stated limitations on structured output and tool use.
headline_results: Limitations section (verbatim gist): DeepSeek-R1's structural output capabilities 'remain suboptimal compared to existing models', and DeepSeek-R1 'cannot leverage tools, such as search engines and calculators'. No function-calling benchmark numbers are reported for the distilled models.
licence: MIT (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: DO NOT use R1-Distill-Qwen-32B as the tool-calling controller. Use it behind a planner/executor split, where Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct emits the JSON calls. If you must use R1-distill for calls, strip the <think> block and force JSON with vLLM guided decoding (json schema / choice over operation names).
risks: Statement concerns R1 itself; distill models inherit training data but were not separately evaluated here.
small_model_evidence: No tool numbers; see Qwen3 report (R1-Distill-Qwen-32B BFCL v3 53.5) and ACBench.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression (ACBench)
core_idea: A benchmark of how quantization, pruning and reasoning-distillation affect agentic skills: workflow generation, tool use (T-Eval), long context and real-world applications. It covers 15 models, including Qwen2.5 7B-32B and the DeepSeek-R1-Distill series.
headline_results: Abstract: 4-bit quantization preserves workflow generation and tool use (1%-3% drop) but degrades real-world application accuracy by 10%-15%. Full text: the R1-Distilled Qwen2.5-7B shows 'a substantial decline in average accuracy from 70% to 43.6%' on tool use vs Qwen2.5-7B. On workflow generation, R1-Distilled-Qwen2.5-7B scores 20% average F1 vs 44% for Qwen2.5-7B. JSON-structured outputs degrade more than string outputs under compression. Qwen2.5-32B keeps its performance under quantization.
licence: MIT (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: EVIDENCE for the planner/executor split: keep R1-distill out of the tool-call path. AWQ/GPTQ 4-bit Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct is a reasonable way to fit a 32B executor on hackathon GPUs. Validate JSON outputs strictly, since compressed models break JSON first.
risks: Distillation numbers are for 7B rather than 32B, and T-Eval is not BFCL.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-7B tool use 70% avg accuracy -> R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 43.6%. Workflow F1 44% -> 20%.

title: Brief Is Better: Non-Monotonic Chain-of-Thought Budget Effects in Function-Calling Language Agents
core_idea: Varies the chain-of-thought token budget before a function call on BFCL v3 'Multiple' tasks. A brief CoT (~32 tokens) helps a lot, while long CoT falls below no-CoT because of function hallucination and misdirection. It proposes Function-Routing CoT (FR-CoT), where the model first names a candidate function, and compares it with log-prob constrained decoding over valid function names.
headline_results: Table 6 (200 BFCL v3 Multiple tasks, greedy). Free-form, budget 0: 44.0% (Qwen2.5-1.5B) / 40.5% (Qwen2.5-7B). Free-form, budget 32: 64.0% / 82.5%. Free-form, budget 256: 25.0% / 18.0%. Constrained decoding: budget 0 47.5% / 58.5%; budget 32 62.5% / 63.5%; budget 256 58.0% / 33.5%. FR-CoT, budget 32: 64.0% / 83.0%, with 0% hallucinated function names. Oracle analysis: 88.6% of tasks are optimally served by <=32 reasoning tokens.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML Tables 3 and 6; budgets read from prose because math tags were stripped)
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT FR-CoT-style routing. Prompt the executor to output a short 'operation: <name>' line (or use vLLM guided_choice over the operation names) before generating args with a JSON schema. Cap reasoning to about 32-64 tokens for the call step. This directly targets near-zero action hallucination.
risks: Single 2026 preprint with small n (200), tested only on 1.5B/7B Qwen2.5 and Phi-3-mini. Effects at 14B-32B are unverified.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on BFCL v3 Multiple: 82.5% with 32-token CoT vs 18.0% with 256-token CoT. Long reasoning hurts function selection, which is relevant for R1-distill models that think at length by default.

title: Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning
core_idea: R1-style GRPO training of Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct with a binary reward (correct format plus a fully correct tool call), using xLAM and ToolACE data and a <think>/<tool_call> template. It needs no distilled reasoning traces.
headline_results: Table 2 (BFCL non-live + live, last updated 2025-04-13; overall): Tool-N1-14B 85.97; Tool-N1-7B 84.82; GPT-4o 83.97; Gemini-2.0-Flash 82.94; ToolACE-8B (FC) 82.57; Hammer2.1-7B (FC) 81.88; GPT-4o-mini 81.64; DeepSeek-R1 80.88; xLAM-2-70b-fc-r (FC) 80.70; Qwen2.5-7B-Inst 76.95; Llama3.1-70B-Inst 76.11; Llama3.1-8B-Inst 72.65. Binary rewards beat fine-grained partial-credit rewards (Table 4).
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW the prompt template (<think> short, then <tool_call>{json}</tool_call>) and the binary call-correctness metric for our eval. RL training is out of scope for 48h.
risks: Excludes BFCL multi-turn, and the scores are not comparable with BFCL v3 overall numbers elsewhere.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 76.95 -> Tool-N1-7B 84.82; Tool-N1-14B (from Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) 85.97 on BFCL single-turn (non-live + live).

title: ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs
venue: NeurIPS 2025 (main track, per NeurIPS proceedings listing)
core_idea: Systematic study of reward design (format plus fine-grained correctness of tool name, param names and values) for GRPO tool-use training from raw instruct models. Evaluated on BFCL v3, API-Bank and Bamboogle.
headline_results: BFCL v3 overall (their prompt): Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct raw 41.97% -> GRPO cold start 58.38%; Qwen2.5-3B raw 33.04% -> 52.98%; Qwen2.5-1.5B raw 19.41% -> 46.20%. Qwen2.5-7B raw multi-turn acc 4.25% (-> 18.12% after GRPO); live acc 53.51% -> 74.9%; irrelevance detection 62.66% -> 76.68%. The text reports ~10% absolute gains over SFT on the same data.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: EVAL INSIGHT: a raw Qwen2.5-7B with a custom prompt scores far lower (41.97) than the leaderboard-style numbers (55.8 in the Qwen3 report). Prompt format alone moves scores by >10 points, so A/B test our tool prompt on our own gold set. Skip RL training for 48h.
risks: Their prompt differs from native FC, and multi-turn stays very low after training.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct raw: BFCL v3 overall 41.97%, non-live AST 66.02%, live 53.51%, multi-turn 4.25%, relevance 76.47%, irrelevance 62.66%.

title: ToolACE: Winning the Points of LLM Function Calling
core_idea: An agentic pipeline synthesizes a 26,507-API pool via self-evolution and builds multi-agent dialogs with dual-layer (rule plus model) verification. LoRA-SFT of LLaMA-3.1-8B on this data (ToolACE-8B) rivals GPT-4 on BFCL.
headline_results: BFCL-v3 (09/20/2024): ToolACE-8B (FC) overall 59.22 (rank 3) vs GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09 (FC) 59.49 (rank 1); ToolACE-8B non-live AST 89.27, exec 90.07, live AST 73.21, multi-turn 14.37, relevance 85.37, irrelevance 83.81. Table 9: RAG-retrieved 3-shot in-context LLaMA-3.1-8B gets non-live(A) 58.81, non-live(E) 53.32, live(A) 36.83, rel 82.93, irrel 23.66. The authors note few-shot ICL 'not only underperforms fine-tuning ... but also falls short of the zero-shot setting', because the model is misled into calling tools from the examples.
implement_or_borrow: KEY FINDING TO APPLY: do not stuff retrieved few-shot examples of other tools into the executor prompt. Use zero-shot with good schemas, or few-shot only on the same operation. ToolACE-2-8B weights are an option for a fast executor if Qwen2.5-14B is too slow.
risks: Evidence is from 8B Llama, and few-shot harm may be smaller at 14B-32B. Model licence not verified.
small_model_evidence: ToolACE-8B BFCL-v3 59.22 overall (multi-turn 14.37). LLaMA-3.1-8B 3-shot RAG ICL irrelevance 23.66 vs fine-tuned 83.81.

title: APIGen: Automated Pipeline for Generating Verifiable and Diverse Function-Calling Datasets
core_idea: Generates function-calling data over 3,673 executable APIs and filters it through three stages: format check, actual execution and semantic verification. The resulting 60k dataset trains the xLAM-1B/7B FC models.
headline_results: BFCL (06/15/2024): xLAM-7B (FC) overall 85.65, rank 6; xLAM-1B (FC) 74.41, rank 24; GPT-4-0125-Preview (Prompt) rank 1 at 88. The base DeepSeek-Coder-v1.5 ranked 45th.
licence: Apache-2.0 for the code repo (read from LICENSE.txt); dataset licence not checked
implement_or_borrow: BORROW the three-stage verifier for our synthetic labelled utterances. Generate NL request -> gold operation call, keep only calls that (1) parse against the op JSON schema, (2) execute on the ERP backend without error and return non-empty data, and (3) pass an LLM check that the result answers the request. This gives a trustworthy gold set for the KPIs in a few hours.
risks: BFCL v1-era scores are inflated compared with v3/v4. xLAM v1 models are DeepSeek-Coder based.
small_model_evidence: xLAM-7B (FC) 85.65 BFCL (v1/v2-era). Leaderboard V4 fetched 2026-10-09 (not paper): xLAM-2-32b-fc-r 54.66%, xLAM-2-8b-fc-r 46.68%.

title: Hammer: Robust Function-Calling for On-Device Language Models via Function Masking
venue: ICLR 2025 (per mlanthology/AMiner listings; OpenReview page not opened)
core_idea: Function-calling models overfit to naming conventions, so performance swings across benchmarks. Hammer masks function and parameter names during training to force reliance on descriptions, and adds 7,500 irrelevance-detection examples to xLAM-60k.
headline_results: Table 5, F1 Func.+Args average over API-Bank L1/L2, Tool-Alpaca, Seal-Tools and Nexus Raven: Qwen2-7B-Instruct 59.84 -> Hammer-7B 76.21; Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct 52.67 -> Hammer-1.5B 66.20; Deepseek-Coder-7B-Instruct 45.67 -> 74.94; xLAM-7B-fc 67.65. Table 1 shows xLAM-7B-fc tops BFCL but has the lowest cross-benchmark average (69.052).
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW the lesson. Write rich descriptions for every operation and do not rely on names like 'analyze' or 'resolve' being self-explanatory. Test robustness by renaming ops in the eval and checking accuracy holds. Also add irrelevant-request examples to the eval.
risks: Results are on Qwen2 (not 2.5) models. On NESTFUL, Hammer2.1-7b scores only 0.08 full-sequence accuracy (3-shot) vs 0.22 for Hammer2.0-7b, so the gains do not carry over to nested calls.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2-7B-Instruct F1 func+args 59.84 -> 76.21 after Hammer tuning.

title: NESTFUL: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Nested Sequences of API Calls
core_idea: 1,800+ executable nested API sequences, where one call's output is an argument to the next call, scored by F1, partial/full sequence accuracy and execution win-rate. Compares direct prompting with ICL against a ReAct agent.
headline_results: Three-shot ICL, full-seq acc / win rate: GPT-4o 0.28 / 0.60; DeepSeek-V3 0.29 / 0.60; Hammer2.0-7b 0.22 / 0.25; Granite-20B-FC 0.21 / 0.20; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 0.16 / 0.11; Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct 0.07 / 0.11; ToolACE-8B 0.00 / 0.00. Win rate, direct one-shot -> ReAct zero-shot: Mixtral-8x22B 0.07 -> 0.30; DeepSeek-V3 0.43 -> 0.46; Hammer2.0-7b 0.16 -> 0.07.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file; the paper also states Apache 2.0)
implement_or_borrow: DESIGN IMPLICATION: avoid relying on the model to chain outputs into inputs (resolve -> analyze). Make the server do the binding, e.g. analyze accepts entity names and resolves them internally, or reference prior results by handle ($1.customer_id) and validate before executing. Add nested multi-step tasks to the eval with full-sequence accuracy.
risks: No Qwen2.5 models are evaluated.
small_model_evidence: Even the best 7-8B models reach at most 0.22 full-sequence accuracy on nested calls (Hammer2.0-7b, 3-shot), and Llama-3.1-70B reaches 0.07.

title: Retrieval Models Aren't Tool-Savvy: Benchmarking Tool Retrieval for Large Language Models (ToolRet)
core_idea: A heterogeneous tool-retrieval benchmark (7.6k tasks, 43k-tool corpus) evaluating sparse, dense, instruction-tuned and reranking retrievers. It shows that strong general IR models do poorly on tools and that this lowers end-to-end agent pass rate. It also releases ToolRet-train (200k+).
headline_results: Avg nDCG@10, query only: NV-Embed-v1 33.83; bge-large-en-v1.5 23.02; BM25s 22.32. With task instruction prepended: NV-Embed-v1 42.71; e5-mistral-7b 38.97; bge-large 38.49; BM25s 36.46. MonoT5 reranking lowers NV-Embed nDCG@10 from 33.83 to 28.92. GPT-3.5 on ToolBench-G1 reaches pass rate 50.60 with bge-large retrieval (-11.40). Training on ToolRet-train raises agent pass rate by 10%-20%.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT hybrid retrieval over pages, widgets and operations: BM25 plus a dense embedder (bge or e5) with the query wrapped in a retrieval instruction. Report P@k, R@k, nDCG@10, MRR and Completeness@k (all needed tools in the top-k) on our own labelled utterances. Do not assume a cross-encoder reranker helps without measuring it.
risks: Corpus is generic APIs. Our page and widget catalogue is smaller and more lexical, so BM25 may be stronger there.
small_model_evidence: Retriever-side only. A 7B embedder (NV-Embed-v1) scores 33.83 nDCG@10 vs 23.02 for bge-large without instructions. Instructions add ~9-16 points.

title: EASYTOOL: Enhancing LLM-based Agents with Concise Tool Instruction
core_idea: An LLM rewrites long, redundant or incomplete tool documentation into a unified, concise 'tool instruction': a description plus functionality guidelines with usage examples. This cuts tokens and reduces wrong tool use.
headline_results: ToolBench doc tokens cut by 70.43%. ToolBench I2-Cat/I3-Inst average (pass / win / success): ChatGPT DFSDT 62.3 / 66.5 / 15.0 -> DFSDT-EasyTool 69.8 / 82.3 / 52.8. Mistral-Instruct-7B and Vicuna-7B score 0.0 with ReAct/DFSDT on raw docs, while Mistral-Instruct-7B with DFSDT-EasyTool scores 70.5 / 81.5 / 47.0. Retrieval (avg NDCG@1/@5): ada embeddings 45.7 / 38.8 -> with EasyTool descriptions 76.7 / 85.6.
licence: MIT (read from the microsoft/JARVIS LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT (about 2h). Use an LLM offline to rewrite every operation, page and widget description into a fixed template: purpose, when to use, when NOT to use, required args with types and enums, and one example call. Embed these rewritten docs for retrieval and put only the top-k into the executor prompt. Expect the biggest gain on 7-14B models.
risks: Old baselines (Vicuna, Mistral-7B), and the evaluation relies on a GPT evaluator.
small_model_evidence: Mistral-Instruct-7B ToolBench avg pass 0.0 -> 70.5 with concise tool instructions.

title: Tool Documentation Enables Zero-Shot Tool-Usage with Large Language Models
core_idea: Shows that zero-shot prompting with tool documentation matches or beats few-shot demonstrations and scales better to large tool sets, where demos cannot cover every tool or flag.
headline_results: On the LLM-Cloud CLI dataset (200 tools), command F1 for text-davinci-002 / gpt-3.5-turbo: zero-shot 0.02 / 0.13; best few-shot without docs 0.05 / 0.19; with docs 0.37 / 0.45. On TabMWP, 0-shot with doc scores 92.69 vs 84.13 without doc (PoT 89.28). On ScienceQA, 79.91 vs 78.25 (CoT 78.54).
implement_or_borrow: Supports doc-first prompting. Give the executor complete arg docs and enums for each retrieved op instead of hand-picked demos.
risks: Uses old closed models only, with no open-model numbers.
small_model_evidence: none (closed models only)

title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
core_idea: Builds ToolBench from 16,464 RapidAPI REST APIs, with ChatGPT-generated instructions and DFSDT (depth-first decision-tree search) solution paths. It fine-tunes LLaMA into ToolLLaMA with a neural API retriever and introduces the ToolEval pass/win-rate evaluator.
headline_results: Table 4, avg pass / win: GPT-4 DFSDT 71.1 / 70.4; ToolLLaMA DFSDT 66.7 / 60.0; ToolLLaMA DFSDT-Retriever 67.3 / 63.1; ChatGPT DFSDT 64.8 / 64.3; ChatGPT ReACT pass 40.2; Vicuna and Alpaca 0.0. Table 2, API retriever avg NDCG@1/@5: BM25 18.5 / 17.0; ada 49.6 / 45.4; their trained retriever 78.0 / 84.9.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW DFSDT-lite: on failure (op error or empty result), backtrack and try the next-best retrieved op instead of giving up. Also the idea of training a small retriever on synthetic (query, op) pairs if time permits.
risks: Real APIs drift, so results are not reproducible (see StableToolBench). LLaMA-1/2-era models.
small_model_evidence: ToolLLaMA-7B DFSDT avg pass 66.7 vs ChatGPT 64.8, while untuned Vicuna/Alpaca-7B score 0.0.

title: StableToolBench: Towards Stable Large-Scale Benchmarking on Tool Learning of Large Language Models
core_idea: Fixes ToolBench instability with a virtual API server (cache plus LLM-simulated APIs) and solvable-only metrics, Solvable Pass Rate (SoPR) and Solvable Win Rate (SoWR), judged by GPT-4.
headline_results: Reproduction on ToolBench I1-Inst: ToolLLaMA v2 DFS reported 57.0 -> reproduced 34.0 (-40.4%); CoT 25.0 -> 15.0. Avg SoPR: gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 DFS 62.2; GPT-4-turbo DFS 60.6; GPT-4-0613 DFS 58.5; ToolLLaMA DFS 46.6; ToolLLaMA CoT 33.9.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW for the eval. Freeze the ERP data snapshot and cache operation responses so KPI runs are deterministic. Score only solvable tasks, and keep a separate 'unanswerable' split for abstention.
risks: LLM-simulated APIs can hide real errors.
small_model_evidence: ToolLLaMA (7B) SoPR 46.6 (DFS) vs GPT-4-0613 58.5.

title: AnyTool: Self-Reflective, Hierarchical Agents for Large-Scale API Calls
core_idea: A hierarchical API retriever (meta-agent -> category agents -> tool agents) over 16k RapidAPI APIs, plus a GPT-4 function-calling solver with self-reflection that re-activates retrieval when a solution fails. The paper also revises ToolBench evaluation to drop unsolvable queries.
headline_results: +35.4% average pass rate over ToolLLM on ToolBench (abstract). Ablation on filtered ToolBench G2-I / G3-I pass rate: AnyTool 58.9 / 63.2; without hierarchical structure 22.4 / 15.8; without self-reflection 19.6 / 15.8; DFSDT replaced by CoT 50.5 / 60.3.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT the hierarchy cheaply. The app's navigation tree is a ready-made category hierarchy (module -> page -> widget/op), so retrieve a module first, then pages, then ops. On empty or failed results, re-retrieve with the failure reason (self-reflection).
risks: All results use GPT-4, and smaller models may not manage multi-agent routing. Cost and latency come from many calls.
small_model_evidence: none (GPT-4 only)

title: Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs
core_idea: Fine-tunes LLaMA-7B on APIBench (HuggingFace, TorchHub and TF Hub API calls) with retriever-aware training, and evaluates by AST sub-tree matching, which also measures hallucinated APIs.
headline_results: Table 1, zero-shot overall / hallucination: TorchHub Gorilla 59.13 / 6.98 vs GPT-4 38.70 / 36.55; HuggingFace Gorilla 71.68 / 10.95 vs GPT-4 19.80 / 37.16; LLAMA 0 / 100. With oracle retrieval, GPT-4 reaches TorchHub 66.12 / 0.53 and HF 85.07 / 10.62. A weak BM25 retriever lowers Gorilla TorchHub to 40.32.
licence: Apache-2.0 (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW the AST-based hallucination metric: share of calls naming an op or arg not in the catalogue. Oracle vs BM25 results show that retrieval quality caps accuracy, so log retrieval recall alongside call accuracy.
risks: Old models and ML-API domain.
small_model_evidence: Fine-tuned LLaMA-7B (Gorilla) reaches hallucination 6.98% vs GPT-4 36.55% zero-shot on TorchHub.

title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
core_idea: A runnable evaluation system with 73 APIs and 314 dialogues (753 calls), graded at three levels: Call, Retrieve+Call, and Plan+Retrieve+Call. It also provides 1,888 training dialogues used to fine-tune Lynx-7B from Alpaca.
headline_results: Table 3, total correctness: GPT-4 60.24%; GPT-3.5-turbo 47.16%; Lynx-7B (fine-tuned) 39.58%; ChatGLM-6B 16.42%; Alpaca-7B 15.19%. Plan+Retrieve+Call: GPT-4 70.00%, GPT-3.5 22.00%, Lynx 20.00%. API-name mismatch is 61% of Lynx errors.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv PDF Table 3 and error analysis)
licence: MIT (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: BORROW the three-level labelling for our utterance set: L1 op given, L2 must retrieve the op, L3 must plan, retrieve and call. Report KPIs per level.
risks: Old models. API-Bank is now used mainly as a secondary benchmark.
small_model_evidence: Lynx-7B 39.58% total vs GPT-3.5 47.16%.

title: RestGPT: Connecting Large Language Models with Real-World RESTful APIs
core_idea: A coarse-to-fine online planner breaks the request into NL sub-tasks. An API selector maps each sub-task to OpenAPI endpoints, and an executor (caller plus schema-based response parser) fills params and extracts fields from JSON. Evaluated on RestBench (TMDB 54 APIs, Spotify 40 APIs, human gold paths).
headline_results: Table 4 (text-davinci-003), success % / correct-path %: TMDB RestGPT 75.0 / 79.0 vs ReAct 44.0 / 57.0 vs Reflexion 52.0 / 59.0; Spotify 72.7 / 74.5 vs ReAct 54.5 / 49.1. Ablations on TMDB: without planner 44.0, without schema parser 46.0. Base LLM: ChatGPT 68.0 (TMDB); Vicuna-13B 9.0; Llama2-13B 0.0.
licence: MIT (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT planner -> selector -> executor -> parser. The schema-based parser (code that extracts fields using the response schema, not the LLM reading raw JSON) is worth ~29 points on TMDB. Have our server ops return compact typed summaries, and let code rather than the LLM reshape the data.
risks: 2023 models: 13B open models failed, though modern Qwen2.5-14B is far stronger. Needs gold paths for the CP metric.
small_model_evidence: Vicuna-13B 9.0% TMDB success; Llama2-13B 0.0% (2023-era models).

title: TinyAgent: Function Calling at the Edge
core_idea: Fine-tunes small models (1.1B, 7B) to emit LLMCompiler-style DAG plans of function calls for a fixed 16-tool macOS assistant. A DeBERTa multi-label classifier (Tool RAG) selects which tool docs go into the prompt, and 4-bit quantization handles deployment.
headline_results: Success rate (plan DAG isomorphic to gold): TinyLlama-1.1B 12.71% -> 78.89%; Wizard-2-7B 41.25% -> 83.09%. Final TinyAgent-1.1B 80.06% and 7B 84.95% vs GPT-4-Turbo 79.08%. Tool RAG classifier picks 3.97 tools/query at recall 0.998 vs basic RAG top-6 at 0.968. 4-bit gives ~30% lower latency.
licence: MIT (read from the repo LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT two ideas: (1) a multi-label classifier, or a few-shot LLM classifier, over our fixed set of operations or pages instead of pure embedding RAG; (2) DAG-plan output so independent ops run in parallel, cutting latency. Use the DAG-isomorphism success metric for multi-step tasks.
risks: Single narrow domain with 16 tools, and fine-tuning needed for the headline numbers.
small_model_evidence: 7B fine-tuned 84.95% vs GPT-4-Turbo 79.08% on an in-domain 16-tool task.

title: Octopus v2: On-device language model for super agent
core_idea: Each function in a fixed API set becomes a special 'functional token', so function selection is a single-token classification by a fine-tuned 2B model. This removes function descriptions from the prompt (95% shorter context).
headline_results: Table 1, Android function-call eval, accuracy / latency: Octopus-0 99.524% / 0.38s; GPT-4 98.571% / 1.02s; GPT-3.5+RAG 98.095% / 1.97s; Llama-7B+RAG 68.095% / 13.46s.
code_url: none found (model released on Hugging Face per paper; not verified)
implement_or_borrow: IDEA ONLY. With a closed set of page routes and operations, constrain decoding to a single choice (vLLM guided_choice) for the destination or operation slot. This gets the 'one token selects the function' benefit without fine-tuning.
risks: Tiny in-domain eval (20 Android APIs), self-reported, and needs fine-tuning.
small_model_evidence: 2B fine-tuned 99.5% on 20 in-domain APIs. Llama-7B+RAG 68.1%.

title: RAG-MCP: Mitigating Prompt Bloat in LLM Tool Selection via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
core_idea: Retrieves the top-k relevant MCP server descriptions from an index before calling the LLM, instead of putting all tool schemas in the prompt. An MCP stress test varies the number of distractors from 1 to 11,100.
headline_results: Table 1, tool-selection accuracy / avg prompt tokens: RAG-MCP 43.13% / 1084; Actual Match 18.20% / 1646; Blank (all tools in prompt) 13.62% / 2133.84. Selection accuracy degrades as the MCP pool grows.
implement_or_borrow: Supports retrieve-then-select over our hundreds of pages and widgets. Never expose the full catalogue to the 14B executor. Pass the top-5 to 10 with docs.
risks: Weak experimental detail, with Qwen-max as retriever and DeepSeek-V3 as judge. Absolute accuracies are low and the setup is ad hoc.
small_model_evidence: none

title: ScaleMCP: Dynamic and Auto-Synchronizing Model Context Protocol Tools for LLM Agents
core_idea: Gives the agent a 'search tools' tool so it can re-query the MCP tool index mid-conversation. The index auto-syncs with MCP servers via CRUD. Tool Document Weighted Average (TDWA) embeddings weight the name and synthetic questions in each tool document.
headline_results: On 5,000 financial-metric MCP servers, vector-only retrieval gives MAP in the ~0.50 range. Best Recall@10 0.94 (VertexAI text-embedding-005 + GPT-4o reranker); best MAP@10 0.59 (same embedding + Claude reranker). BM25 is weakest. Adding 10 synthetic questions per tool doc consistently improves retrieval.
implement_or_borrow: IMPLEMENT synthetic-question enrichment. For each page, widget and op, generate about 10 example user questions, embed them with the doc, and expose 'search_capabilities(query)' as a tool so the agent can retrieve again during multi-step tasks.
risks: Agents evaluated are all closed models, and the multi-hop queries need 3-12 tools each.
small_model_evidence: none (closed models only)

title: Small Reasoning Models are Instruction Followers in Function Calling
core_idea: Function calling is more accurate when posed as plain instruction following (prompt-based, from a small dedicated model) than through native tool-calling templates. IFFC moves tool selection to a small model and appends the tool results to the main LLM's query.
headline_results: Table 2, BFCL V3 avg accuracy, IFFC / prompt FC / native FC. Live: Qwen-3 8B Think 83.3 / 78.3 / 75.5; Qwen-3 4B Think 86.7 / 82.8 / 81.5; Phi-4 Mini 44.3 / 62.5 / 30.0. Non-Live: Qwen-3 8B Think 94.9 / 89.7 / 88.8; Phi-4 Mini 77.4 / 41.9 / 9.5.
implement_or_borrow: SUPPORTS the planner/executor split. A dedicated executor model receives only the selected op docs, and its output feeds the main reasoning model, which never sees raw tool schemas. Also A/B test vLLM native tool parser vs a plain JSON prompt.
risks: Very recent, unrefereed preprint evaluated on Qwen3 and Phi-4 Mini, not Qwen2.5 or R1-distill.
small_model_evidence: Native FC can collapse for some small models (Phi-4 Mini non-live 9.5 native vs 77.4 IFFC). Qwen3-8B gains 5-8 points with prompt-style calls.

title: AppWorld: A Controllable World of Apps and People for Benchmarking Interactive Coding Agents
core_idea: A 60K-LOC engine of 9 day-to-day apps exposed through 457 APIs, populated with ~100 simulated users, plus 750 tasks that agents solve by writing interactive code against the APIs. Evaluation is state-based: a hash-based DB diff between start and final state is checked by programmatic unit tests for expected changes AND for absence of any non-allowed change (collateral damage).
headline_results: 750 tasks (Test-Normal / Test-Challenge). GPT-4o + ReAct: TGC 48.8 (Test-N) / 30.2 (Test-C); scenario-level SGC for GPT-4o drops to 32.1 / 13.0. Next best GPT-4-Turbo 32.7 / 17.5 TGC. CodeAct (Mistral-7B) and ToolLLaMA: 0.0 on all tasks.
verification: verified-abstract (task/API counts, ~49%/~30%); verified-fulltext (Table 3 numbers, Sec 3.2 evaluation: C_expect subset of D_delta subset of C_expect U C_allow)
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file in repo root, checked via raw.githubusercontent)
implement_or_borrow: COPY the DB-diff evaluator: snapshot ERP DB before task, compute row-level diff after, assert (a) every expected change present (C_expect, e.g. exactly one PO created with qty=X) and (b) diff contains nothing outside C_expect U C_allow (collateral damage, e.g. no other orders edited). Also copy Task Goal Completion vs Scenario Goal Completion: group 3+ paraphrased/variant tasks per scenario and count a scenario as passed only if all variants pass. Pair each assertion with a natural-language statement for readable failure reports.
risks: Writing C_allow sets per task is manual effort; for read-only analytical tasks the diff is empty so answer-checking must be separate. Code-generation agent style differs from named-operation tool calling.
hybrid_evidence: N/A (pure API environment; no UI layer).
small_model_evidence: Llama-3-70B (FullCodeRefl) TGC 24.4 Test-N / 7.0 Test-C (best open); Llama-3-70B ReAct 20.8 / 3.4; DeepSeek-Coder-33B FullCodeRefl 13.1 / 5.8, ReAct 7.1 / 2.9. Greedy decoding.

title: tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
core_idea: An LLM-simulated user converses with a function-calling agent that has domain API tools and a written policy (retail, airline). Success = final database state equals the annotated goal state, and reliability is measured with pass^k: probability that all k i.i.d. trials of the same task succeed.
headline_results: tau-retail 115 tasks, tau-airline 50 tasks. pass^1 (FC): gpt-4o 61.2 retail / 35.2 airline (avg 48.2); claude-3-opus 44.2 / 34.7. gpt-4o pass^8 < 25% on retail. Removing policy from prompt drops gpt-4o by 22.4 points on airline.
verification: verified-abstract (DB-state eval, pass^k, <50%, pass^8<25%); verified-fulltext (Table 1 task counts, Table 2 numbers, pass^k formula)
implement_or_borrow: COPY pass^k with the unbiased estimator pass^k = E_task[C(c,k)/C(n,k)] from n>=k trials per task (n=4..8 at temperature>0 or with paraphrased user turns) - report pass^1 and pass^4 side by side for intent routing and UI-state tasks. COPY 'only one valid end state' task authoring: write each task so policy + user intent determine a unique final DB/UI state, enabling exact state comparison instead of LLM judging. Also copy the policy-removal ablation to test whether the agent actually uses the app's metadata/policy doc.
risks: User simulator is itself noisy (tau2 paper measured 40%/47% user-sim error rates in retail/airline). Small task count means wide CIs. Exact-state match penalises harmless extra reads only if they write.
small_model_evidence: meta-llama-3-70B (text ReAct) pass^1 14.8 retail / 14.4 airline (avg 14.6); mixtral-8x22b 17.7 / 31.6 (avg 24.7). Paper states it did not test 7/13B models due to difficulty.

title: tau^2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
core_idea: Extends tau-bench with a telecom domain modelled as a Dec-POMDP where both agent and simulated user call tools on a shared world state, plus a compositional task generator built from atomic subtasks with init/solution/assertion functions. Adds No-User and oracle-plan ablations to separate reasoning errors from communication/coordination errors.
headline_results: Telecom: 2285 programmatically composed tasks, subsampled to 114. gpt-4.1 pass^1 drops from 74% (retail) / 56% (airline) to 34% (telecom); gpt-4.1-mini, o4-mini, claude-3.7-sonnet ~50% on telecom. Each task run 4 times. User-sim error rate 40% retail, 47% airline (12%/13% critical) vs 16% telecom (6% critical).
verification: verified-abstract; verified-fulltext (Sec 3-5: success criteria list, task counts, pass^1 numbers, user-sim error table)
implement_or_borrow: COPY the multi-criterion success check: DB check + status assertions on final world state + natural-language assertions on conversation history + communication-info check + action matching. For VACP, the 'shared state' idea maps directly: the user may also click filters, so assert on getState() after the dialogue. COPY the compositional generator: define atomic sub-intents (navigate, set date range, set filter, sort, read widget) each with init/solution/assert functions and combine them programmatically to get hundreds of verifiable multi-step tasks. COPY No-User mode (give agent the full task directly) to isolate planning errors from dialogue errors.
risks: Only proprietary models evaluated; telecom domain far from analytics. Dual-control adds simulator complexity we may not need.
hybrid_evidence: Dual-control shared state is analogous to a user and agent both manipulating the same UI; no direct UI evidence.
small_model_evidence: None printed (gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, o4-mini, claude-3.7-sonnet only).

title: WorkArena: How Capable Are Web Agents at Solving Common Knowledge Work Tasks?
core_idea: 33 task types (19,912 instances) on a real ServiceNow instance covering list filtering/sorting, forms, knowledge base, service catalog, dashboard reading and menu navigation, run via the BrowserGym environment. Each task implements setup(), teardown(), validate() and an optional cheat() oracle; validation queries the DB, checks URL/page content, or checks the chat answer.
headline_results: WorkArena (33 tasks): GPT-4o 43% success, GPT-3.5 6.1%, Llama3-70B 17.9% (abstract-level: big open/closed gap). Dashboard tasks validated by checking the answer contains key numbers/labels of chart elements.
verification: verified-abstract (33 tasks, BrowserGym, open/closed gap); verified-fulltext (19,912 instances, task categories, setup/teardown/validate/cheat API, 43%/6.1%/17.9%)
implement_or_borrow: COPY the 4-function task contract for our runner: setup() seeds DB/UI state and opens start route; validate() returns (reward, msg, done) by checking DB, current URL/route, getState() widget state, and agent chat; cheat() is a scripted oracle that solves the task via the same VACP execute() calls - run cheat() in CI to prove every task is solvable before scoring agents; teardown() resets. COPY task families that mirror our UI: list filter (1-5 conditions), sort (up to 3 columns), dashboard value read (answer must contain specific numbers/labels), menu navigation (assert final route).
risks: Requires ServiceNow developer instance; UI-level (AXTree) rather than API-level. Template-generated goals explicitly give all info, so intent ambiguity is not tested.
hybrid_evidence: Validators check both backend DB and frontend page state - a hybrid API+UI validation pattern directly reusable for VACP.
small_model_evidence: Llama3-70B (8K context, TGI on 4xA100) 17.9% on WorkArena; Llama2: 0% in preliminary experiments. Chain-of-thought removal drops Llama3 ~10 points.

title: WorkArena++: Towards Compositional Planning and Reasoning-based Common Knowledge Work Tasks
core_idea: Composes WorkArena L1 oracles/validators into 341 workflows, each presented at L2 (explicit step instructions) and L3 (implicit goal via ticket + knowledge base), for 682 tasks over 5 skill categories incl. retrieval and data-driven decision-making. Includes a human study and generation of oracle traces for fine-tuning.
headline_results: 682 tasks. Agent curriculum: GPT-4o 3.0% on L2 (235 instances), 0.0% on L3; Llama3 and Mixtral 0.0 on both. Human curriculum (98 instances, 15 subjects): humans 93.9% vs GPT-4o 2.1%.
verification: verified-abstract (682 tasks); verified-fulltext (L2/L3 definitions, Table 2 numbers, human study)
implement_or_borrow: COPY the explicit-vs-implicit split: author each multi-step analytics task twice - L2 with step list ('open Inventory page, set warehouse=W1, sort by stock asc') and L3 with only the business goal ('which W1 SKUs are at risk of stock-out?') - the gap measures intent-to-destination planning vs execution. COPY composition of validated atomic tasks into workflows so validators are reused. COPY a small human baseline on a subset with the identical interface.
risks: Near-zero agent scores give little signal for small models; ServiceNow dependency.
hybrid_evidence: Validation inspects DB via REST and page via frontend JS APIs (hybrid).
small_model_evidence: Llama3-70B and Mixtral-8x22B: 0.0% on both L2 and L3.

title: ToolSandbox: A Stateful, Conversational, Interactive Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Tool Use Capabilities
core_idea: A Python-native stateful tool environment (34 tools, 11 domains) with an LLM user simulator and 1032 expert-written scenarios, including implicit state dependencies (e.g., cellular must be on before messaging) and insufficient-information scenarios. Trajectories are scored against Milestones (DAG of required events with similarity measures) and Minefields (events that must never occur; any hit zeroes the score).
headline_results: 1032 scenarios. Avg similarity: GPT-4o-2024-05-13 73.0 (best); GPT-4o on Insufficient Information category 42.0. Best open model Hermes-2-Pro-Mistral-7B 31.4, >20 points behind Claude-3-Haiku. Larger models (GPT-4, Claude-3-Opus) do worse on State Dependency due to erroneous parallel tool calls.
verification: verified-abstract; verified-fulltext (Table 5 numbers, milestone/minefield definitions, 1032 scenarios, 34 tools)
licence: Apple custom licence (LICENSE begins 'Copyright (C) 2024 Apple Inc. All Rights Reserved. IMPORTANT: This Apple software is supplied...') - not an OSI SPDX licence; review before reuse
implement_or_borrow: COPY Milestones as a DAG of required intermediate events (e.g., M1 navigate(/inventory) -> M2 set_filter(warehouse=W1) -> M3 read_widget(stock_grid)) matched with per-milestone similarity, giving partial credit and order checking over any trajectory. COPY Minefields to measure action hallucination: for infeasible requests (filter value that does not exist, page not in nav tree, write op without confirmation) define forbidden calls; any minefield hit -> score 0. Directly yields our 'near-zero action hallucination' KPI. COPY tool augmentations (distractor tools, scrambled names/descriptions) to test retrieval over hundreds of operations.
risks: Milestone authoring needs deep tool knowledge (authors note scalability limits). Similarity metric gives soft scores that need thresholds.
small_model_evidence: Hermes-2-Pro-Mistral-7B 31.4; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 29.8 (but 76.8 on Insufficient Information, i.e., refuses often); C4AI-Command-R 26.2; Gorilla-Openfunctions-v2 25.6; Command R+ 24.7.

title: WorkBench: a Benchmark Dataset for Agents in a Realistic Workplace Setting (+ WorkBench Revisited, arXiv 2606.13715)
core_idea: Sandbox of five databases (incl. website analytics, CRM, calendar, email, project management), 26 tools and 690 tasks, some conditional on analytics (e.g., 'if page views fell >10% last week, schedule a meeting, else email'). Outcome-centric evaluation compares the final state of all databases with a unique ground-truth outcome and separately counts side effects (wrong DB changes).
headline_results: 690 tasks. 2024: GPT-4 43% (all tools) / 49% (required tools only); Llama2-70B 3%/0%; Mixtral-8x7B 20%/16%. Revisited (2606.13715, June 2026): best 'Claude Fable 5' 97.7% completion, 1.9% harmful side effects; GPT-4 side effects fell from 26% (2024) to 1.9% for best model.
verification: verified-abstract (both papers); verified-fulltext (Table 5 of 2405.00823; Table 1 of 2606.13715)
implement_or_borrow: COPY the two-metric pair: accuracy (outcome == ground truth across ALL DBs) and side-effect rate (DB changed but not equal to ground truth) - side-effect rate is a direct operationalisation of 'action hallucination'. COPY conditional analytics->action tasks where the ground-truth outcome is computed by a small Python function over the seeded data, so the expected state is regenerated automatically. COPY 'required tools only' vs 'all tools' condition to measure the effect of tool retrieval.
risks: Synthetic data; benchmark now near-saturated for frontier models (98%), but still discriminative for small open models.
small_model_evidence: 2024: Llama2-70B 3% (required tools), Mixtral-8x7B 20%. 2026 Revisited: Kimi-K2.6 88.0% (6.8% side effects), DeepSeek-V4-pro 84.2%, GLM-4.6 77.4%, Qwen3.5 70.7% (21.4% side effects, $0.003/task).

title: CRMArena: Understanding the Capacity of LLM Agents to Perform Professional CRM Tasks in Realistic Environments
core_idea: A Salesforce Service Cloud sandbox with 16 interconnected objects and latent variables, and nine expert-validated tasks across service agent, analyst and manager personas, solved via SOQL/SOSL queries or task-specific function wrappers. Includes non-answerable (false-presupposition) queries; scoring is exact match on object IDs and F1 for knowledge QA.
headline_results: 9 tasks. Best ReAct: o1 57.7% overall; with human-crafted functions best overall 64.3%. gpt-4o FC 54.4%. Weaker models do worse with function calling than with prompting.
verification: verified-abstract (<40% ReAct, <55% FC for SOTA at time); verified-fulltext (Table 2 numbers, metrics)
licence: CC-BY-NC-4.0 (LICENSE.txt in repo); HF dataset Salesforce/CRMArena tagged cc-by-nc-4.0 - non-commercial
implement_or_borrow: COPY persona-based task families for analytics: 'analyst' tasks whose answer is an ID/number checked by exact match after an answer-extractor, e.g. 'which supplier had most late POs in Q3?' -> supplier_id. COPY unanswerable false-presupposition queries (ask about a page/metric/period that doesn't exist) and score refusal. COPY the Act vs ReAct vs function-calling comparison to decide whether Qwen2.5-14B should use native FC or prompted JSON.
risks: Requires Salesforce org for live env; NC licence restricts commercial reuse. Exact-match on IDs ignores explanation faithfulness.
small_model_evidence: ReAct overall: llama3.1-405b 33.8, llama3.1-70b 27.8, llama3.1-8b 3.1, deepseek-r1 35.1. FC (prompt mode): llama3.1-405b 51.3, llama3.1-70b 41.1, llama3.1-8b 0.0, deepseek-r1 9.0.

title: CRMArena-Pro: Holistic Assessment of LLM Agents Across Diverse Business Scenarios and Interactions
core_idea: Expands CRMArena to 19 expert-validated tasks across sales, service and CPQ for B2B and B2C orgs, in single-turn and multi-turn (persona-driven simulated user) settings. Adds confidentiality-awareness probes (PII, internal data) scored by an LLM judge.
headline_results: 4,280 queries (100 per task per org + 80 confidentiality queries per org per aspect). Single-turn: gemini-2.5-pro 54.1 (B2B) / 58.3 (B2C); multi-turn drops to 35.1 / 30.0. Workflow Execution >83% single-turn for top agents. Near-zero inherent confidentiality awareness.
verification: verified-abstract (~58% single, ~35% multi); verified-fulltext (Table 2 numbers, query counts, metric definitions)
implement_or_borrow: COPY single-turn vs multi-turn versions of the same task (multi-turn: simulated user reveals constraints gradually) to measure clarification handling. COPY skill taxonomy for reporting (Workflow execution, Policy compliance, Text reasoning, Database/analytics querying) - break our KPI dashboard down by skill. COPY confidentiality probes as guardrail tests (e.g., asking for supplier bank details or another tenant's data must be refused).
risks: LLM judge for confidentiality; NC licence.
small_model_evidence: Single-turn All: llama4-maverick 32.6 (B2B) / 37.5 (B2C); llama3.1-405b 28.7 / 26.5; llama3.1-70b 25.2 / 24.9. Multi-turn: llama4-maverick 23.7 / 14.9; llama3.1-70b 16.3 (B2B).

title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
core_idea: A self-hosted simulated software company (GitLab, Plane, ownCloud, RocketChat with LLM colleague NPCs) and 175 professional tasks spanning SWE, PM, HR, admin and finance. Each task has weighted checkpoints evaluated by deterministic programs or rubric-based LLM evaluators, giving both full and partial-credit scores.
headline_results: 175 tasks. Gemini-2.5-Pro (OpenHands 0.28.1) 30.3% full completion, 39.3% partial score; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 26.3% / 36.4%; GPT-4o 8.6% / 16.7%.
verification: verified-abstract (30% best); verified-fulltext (Table 1, S_partial formula, checkpoint design)
implement_or_borrow: COPY S_partial = 0.5*(points_earned/total_points) + 0.5*S_full, with checkpoint weights by importance - rewards progress on long multi-step analyses while still heavily favouring full completion. COPY reporting steps and cost per task alongside success (our latency KPI). COPY a second-person audit of checkpoint weights for consistency.
risks: Heavy environment (multiple self-hosted services); LLM evaluators on unstructured deliverables add judge noise.
hybrid_evidence: Agents use both browser and APIs/code in the same tasks (OpenHands), but no controlled API-vs-UI comparison.

title: ST-WebAgentBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Safety and Trustworthiness in Web Agents
core_idea: Pairs enterprise web tasks (GitLab, ShoppingAdmin, SuiteCRM) with explicit safety/trust policies across six dimensions (user consent, boundary, strict execution, hierarchy, robustness, error handling). Introduces Completion under Policy (CuP), which credits a completion only if no policy is violated, plus partial CuP and per-dimension Risk Ratio.
headline_results: Abstract (latest version): 222 tasks; full text (current HTML): 375 tasks with 3,057 policy instances (discrepancy between abstract and body). Across 3 agents (gpt-4o backbone, pass@3): mean CR 24.3% vs CuP 15.0% (~38% relative drop); CuP falls from 18.2% with 1 policy to 7.1% with 5+. AWM: CR 33.8%, CuP 20%, PCR 46.9%.
verification: verified-abstract (CuP definition, 'CuP < 2/3 of CR'); verified-fulltext (CuP formula, 375 tasks, 24.3/15.0, policy-load numbers)
licence: Apache (LICENSE text: 'All code and data is licensed under the Apache License'; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
implement_or_borrow: COPY CuP_t = C_t * 1[sum_d V_d^t = 0]: a task counts only if completed AND zero policy violations. Our policies: 'ask_user before any state-changing execute()', 'never touch pages outside allowed nav subtree', 'do not change filters the user did not mention'. Report CR and CuP side by side plus Risk Ratio per policy dimension. COPY stratification by number of active policies. COPY the explicit ask_the_user action so consent is machine-checkable.
risks: Only gpt-4o-backed agents evaluated; numbers use pass@3 (optimistic). Task count inconsistency across versions.
hybrid_evidence: Policies enforced on UI agents via BrowserGym; directly transferable to VACP execute() gating.
small_model_evidence: None (only gpt-4o-backed agents; WebArena leaderboard table in appendix lists others but not on this benchmark).

title: EntWorld: A Holistic Environment and Benchmark for Verifiable Enterprise GUI Agents
core_idea: 1,756 GUI tasks over six open-source enterprise systems (EspoCRM, ZenTao, OpenProject, Veops CMDB, Snipe-IT, iTop) generated by reverse-engineering business workflows from DB schemas. Each task carries ground-truth SQL; verification is SQL-based state checking, with CUD tasks validated inside a transaction then rolled back.
headline_results: 1,756 tasks. GPT-4.1 47.61% SR ($0.16/task); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 28.78% (partial subset); estimated human 85.00%. Authors' EntAgent-RL (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) 56.89%, EntAgent-SFT 50.57%. (Body text contains an inconsistent sentence saying GPT-4.1 47.61% is 'lower than the human performance of 37.39%'; Table 1 says 85.00 estimated.)
verification: verified-abstract (1,756 tasks, 47.61%); verified-fulltext (Table 1, SQL verification, transaction-rollback validation)
code_url: None found: paper body contains no code/data URL; GitHub search finds no official repo (the github org 'entworld/entworld.github.io' is an unrelated spam site); no HF dataset. Abstract says 'We release EntWorld' but nothing public was located on 2026-10-09.
implement_or_borrow: COPY schema-grounded task generation: from the ERP schema (orders, inventory, POs, invoices) infer FK joins, verify each join with a probe SQL returning non-empty rows, then have an LLM produce task templates with ground-truth SQL + placeholders; validate executability inside a transaction and ROLLBACK. Gives hundreds of verified analytical tasks quickly. COPY 'ground-truth SQL as oracle answer' for analytical faithfulness: compare the agent's numbers to the SQL result.
risks: No public release; internal inconsistency in human-performance text; appendix per-system counts reportedly sum to 1,751 not 1,756 (per secondary summary, not re-checked).
hybrid_evidence: GUI tasks verified by backend SQL (UI action, DB verification) - same hybrid pattern as VACP + server DB.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct 23.97%; UI-TARS-72B-DPO (Qwen2-VL-72B) 34.51%; WebRL-8B (Llama-3.1-8B) 2.51%; WebRL-9B (GLM-4-9B) 18.34%; EntAgent-RL (Qwen2.5-VL-32B, SFT+RL) 56.89%.

title: EnterpriseOps-Gym: Environments and Evaluations for Stateful Agentic Planning and Tool Use in Enterprise Settings
core_idea: Containerised sandbox with 164 DB tables and 512 tools across eight enterprise verticals (Customer Service, HR, IT, Email, Calendar, hybrid, ...) and 1,150 expert-curated tasks including 30 infeasible tasks. Expert-written executable SQL verifiers check goal completion, state integrity, policy compliance and side effects; human oracle plans enable a planning ablation.
headline_results: 1,150 tasks. Best Claude Opus 4.5 37.4% (avg pass@1 over 3 runs, all verifiers must pass). Oracle human plans add 14-35 points. Best infeasible-task refusal 53.9%.
verification: verified-abstract; verified-fulltext (Table 2 open-model numbers, SQL verifier description, pass@1 averaged over 3 runs)
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo LICENSE; HF dataset tag license:apache-2.0)
implement_or_borrow: COPY per-task SQL verifier sets (goal, integrity, policy, side-effect checks; ~10 checks per infeasible task) with task success = all verifiers pass, and also report verifier-level pass rate for partial signal. COPY the oracle-plan ablation: give the agent a human-written plan to separate planning failure from execution failure. COPY a dedicated infeasible-task slice scored on correct refusal with zero side effects.
risks: Large environment; most domains are ITSM/HR rather than analytics.

Ground truth is regenerated on demand by replaying expert tool-call trajectories against the current environment; an LLM judge scores answer correctness (Pass@k) and trajectory coverage.

code_url: None found (no repo URL in paper; GitHub search negative)
