title: SaaS-Bench: Can Computer-Use Agents Leverage Real-World SaaS to Solve Professional Workflows?
core_idea: 106 long-horizon tasks over 23 deployable SaaS systems in six professional domains, executed by browser-use agents. Each task has weighted checkpoints verified by State-Check (DB records, API responses, files), Content-Check (rules/string match) or LLM-Judge, aggregated to a strict Resolved Score and a partial Checkpoint Score.

COPY the p^N argument for task design: with 12 checkpoints at p=0.95 full success is ~54%, so keep multi-step tasks short or report partial credit. COPY checkpoint-position analysis (early/middle/late) to show where long analyses break.

hybrid_evidence: Browser agents act on UI while checkpoints verify backend state (hybrid validation).

title: MCPMark: A Benchmark for Stress-Testing Realistic and Comprehensive MCP Use

verification: verified-abstract; verified-fulltext (environments, verification scripts, open-model numbers, Table 2 caption)

COPY reporting pass@1 (mean of 4), pass@4 and pass^4 together, plus turns/tool-calls per task and a failure taxonomy (malformed call, turn limit, context overflow, premature stop, implicit).

title: MCP-Universe: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Real-World Model Context Protocol Servers
core_idea: 231 tasks over 11 real MCP servers in 6 domains (location navigation, repository management, financial analysis, 3D design, browser automation, web search). Uses execution-based evaluators: format evaluators, static evaluators, and dynamic evaluators that fetch real-time ground truth, explicitly rejecting LLM-as-judge.

verification: verified-abstract; verified-fulltext (231 tasks, Table 3 open-model SR, evaluator types)

Report Average Evaluator score (fraction of evaluators passed) alongside SR, plus avg steps for successful tasks. COPY the 'add unrelated servers' ablation for tool-retrieval robustness.

hybrid_evidence: Browser automation domain via Playwright MCP alongside API domains.

title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
core_idea: Connects agents to 28 live MCP servers with 250 tools; tasks are LLM-synthesised from dependency-chain analysis and then 'fuzzed' so they don't name tools. Scoring mixes rule-based execution metrics (name validity, schema adherence, runtime success, dependency compliance) with a rubric LLM judge given the hidden unfuzzed task and dependency analysis.
headline_results: 104 tasks (56 single-server, 30 two-server, 18 three-server). Overall score: gpt-5 0.749, o3 0.715, gpt-oss-120b 0.692; llama-3-1-8b-instruct 0.428. Strong models >98% schema compliance; planning (dependency awareness, parallelism) is the differentiator.

licence: Apache-2.0 (seen on GitHub repo page; API rate-limited so not double-checked via API)
implement_or_borrow: COPY fuzzy-instruction tasks: write the business goal without naming pages/operations, while the judge sees the concrete version - directly tests intent-to-destination. COPY rule-based tool metrics computed from traces (valid op name rate, schema-valid args rate, runtime success rate, dependency compliance) - cheap, judge-free, and they quantify action hallucination (invalid op/param = hallucination).

small_model_evidence: Overall: qwen3-235b-a22b-2507 0.678, qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct-2507 0.627, llama-3-3-70b-instruct 0.558, llama-3-1-8b-instruct 0.428 (0.438 single-server -> 0.415 multi-server).

title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
core_idea: 1,000 human-written tasks over 36 real MCP servers and 220 tools, with prompts that do not name servers/tools and include plausible distractors. Each task is scored with a claim-level rubric (atomic factual claims grounded in tool outputs, fulfilled/partial/not), letting alternative trajectories earn credit, plus an 11-category failure taxonomy.
headline_results: 1,000 tasks (500 public / 500 private). Best pass rate 82.2% at 0.75 claim-coverage threshold (Muse Spark), Claude Opus 4.7 79.1%, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview 78.2%. 63.3% of diagnosed failures are cognitive rather than tool-call related. Mean 4.7 claims per task.
verification: verified-abstract; verified-fulltext (claim scoring, model numbers, public/private split)
implement_or_borrow: COPY claim-level faithfulness scoring for analytical answers: for each analysis task list 3-6 atomic claims grounded in data-view outputs (e.g., 'Q3 revenue = 1.24M', 'decline driven by region North'), judge each claim 1/0.5/0, pass if coverage >= 0.75. This is our 'analytical faithfulness' KPI. COPY public/private task split with a >6pp gap as a contamination/overfitting audit trigger. COPY cross-judge agreement check (rankings across 2-3 judge models).

small_model_evidence: GLM-5.1 75.6% (strongest open, statistically tied with GPT-5.5); GLM-4.7 and Kimi K2.5 also evaluated (numbers not extracted).

title: VACP: Visual Analytics Context Protocol
core_idea: An in-app protocol that makes visual analytics apps 'agent-ready' by exposing (1) a semantic application state (a hierarchical capability graph of nodes/edges with stable refs plus a timestamped state snapshot), (2) the currently valid interactions with typed parameter schemas, and (3) an execution gateway that validates and runs semantic actions and returns structured success/error feedback. Data stays out of the state (details-on-demand): agents call schema/query actions to pull only the rows/aggregates they need, and MCP is used purely as a thin transport with a small static tool set.
headline_results: Benchmark: 5 use cases x 3 tasks (locate/identify/compare) = 15 tasks, 3 runs per model, ReAct loop in OpenCode. Overall success per model (Fig. 6, read from the published figure): S1 UI+DOM baseline: Claude Sonnet 4.5 28.89%, Gemini 3 Pro Preview 46.67%, GPT-5.2 51.11%; S2 UI+DOM+state-in-DOM: 31.11% / 51.11% / 51.11%; S3 VACP-only: 91.11% / 100.00% / 97.78%; S4 VACP+UI+DOM: 100.00% / 95.56% / 95.56%. Text: S1 28%-51%; S2 31%-51% (max gain 4.4%); S3/S4 'near-perfect'. Efficiency (text): S3 used significantly fewer tokens and finished faster than S1, S2, S4; Claude <2000 tokens in S3 vs >30000 for GPT-5.2 in S3; S4 consistently increased tokens and time vs S3 'typically without a proportional increase in success rate'. Fig. 7 (median tokens vs median duration; values only approximately readable from the plot): all VACP scenarios (S3,S4) sit below ~170 s median duration while all non-VACP (S1,S2) are above it; Gemini S1 ~200k tokens/~600 s vs S3 ~85k/~130 s; Claude S1 ~10k/~280 s vs S3 ~1.7k/~50 s. Human expert study: N=7, 85.71% completion. Turn-annotation reliability Cohen's kappa=0.918 on 20% sample.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v1 read in full incl. Sections 3-6; Fig. 6/7 SVGs rendered and read; repo README, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/reference/tool-contract.md and packages/lib/protocol/core/src/schema.ts read)
licence: none declared (GitHub API license=null; no LICENSE file in repo tree on main) - treat as all-rights-reserved; borrow design, not code, unless authors add a licence
implement_or_borrow: Paper method names (snake_case): get_state(), get_capabilities(), execute_interaction(), get_schema(), inspect_data(), get_chart() (L1 screenshot), get_dom_extract() (L2). Repo bridge (ARCHITECTURE.md conformance, 'MUST'): window.__vacp = {version, getCapabilities(request?), getState(request?), execute(call)} - the team's {getCapabilities,getState,execute} matches the repo exactly. Implement from schema.ts: VacpRef='vacp://...' stable ids (never DOM order); VacpNode{ref,kind,layer,title?,description?,data?} with kinds App/View/Visualization/Mark/EncodingChannel/EncodedField/Legend/Axis/Selection/Param/Widget/DataHandle/InteractionTarget and layers ConfigLayer/ViewLayer/VisualizationLayer/DataLayer/InteractionFeedbackLayer; VacpEdge{from,to,kind in contains|controls|derivedFrom|targets}; VacpActionDescriptor{name,title?,description,parameters (JSON-schema-like),targetRef?}; VacpCapabilitiesSnapshot{version,createdAt,graph{nodes,edges,actions}}; VacpCapabilitiesRequest{refs,prefixes,kinds,layers,includeActions,includeEdges,includeNodeData} for scoped (token-cheap) reads; VacpStateRequest{mode:'auto'|'full'|'delta', since(token), refs, includeSummary} returning full snapshot+token or delta{changed,removed} with baseToken (deterministic hash) - use delta mode to keep tokens low; VacpActionCall{callId,name,params}; VacpActionResult {callId,ok:true,result} | {callId,ok:false,error{message,details}}. Standard actions to mirror: vacp.apply_state (desired state map keyed by ref; returns refs it could not apply), vacp.data_schema (columns/types/rowCount, numeric min/max/avg, temporal min/max, categorical top values), vacp.data_sql (SQL over 'vacp_handle' = filtered relation and 'vacp_all' = unfiltered, maxRows, truncated flag) - map to ERP data handles so arithmetic is done by the engine, not the LLM. Gateway must: resolve action ref, check it is still valid in the current snapshot, type/range-check params, execute, return structured error for self-correction; optional undo/redo, provenance log and human-confirmation hooks for high-stakes actions. Expose a small static tool set (vacp_capabilities, vacp_state, vacp_execute(name, params, call_id)) instead of one tool per action.

Token savings are model-dependent (Gemini S3 ~85k median tokens is higher than Claude S1 ~10k; GPT S4 appears to use more tokens than GPT S1 in Fig. 7). Authors note developer overhead of mapping state/actions and LLM inference latency as bottlenecks. No licence on code.
hybrid_evidence: S4 (VACP + screenshots + DOM) vs S3 (VACP only): S4 success 100/95.56/95.56% vs S3 91.11/100/97.78% (mixed), but S4 consistently costs more tokens and time. Agents in S4 used semantic calls first, then pragmatic (pixel) calls to verify; authors recommend a 'dual-channel' design: API-driven semantic layer for execution plus deterministic visual feedback for verification.
small_model_evidence: Only a qualitative sentence: 'Preliminary experiments with smaller, on-device LLMs using VACP also showed promising success' - no models or numbers reported. All quantitative results use GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro Preview.

title: EmbeWebAgent: Embedding Web Agents into Any Customized UI
venue: arXiv preprint (Technical Report; IBM Research Europe)
core_idea: Embed an agent in an existing enterprise UI via a small frontend shim that exposes curated ARIA-label + URL observations and a per-page function registry (names, schemas, page associations) over a WebSocket, while all reasoning lives in a reusable backend. A web-interaction agent picks from page-filtered functions (mixed granularity: GUI primitives plus composites, plus an explicit navigate(url) action listing all reachable URLs), an analysis agent calls domain tools via MCP, and a chat agent summarises.
headline_results: No quantitative benchmark results. Reported engineering numbers: frontend shim ~150 lines of code, function registry ~200 lines (demo). Works with React and Angular; demo uses Llama 4 Maverick via watsonx.ai with DSPy. Evaluation is an integration test suite (pytest/pytest-asyncio/assertpy) checking function calls/parameters or navigation to target URLs, exact-match or LLM-judged similarity for chat, Phoenix tracing for latency and session isolation - no scores reported.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v1, full paper read)
code_url: none found in paper (live demo video https://youtu.be/Cy06Ljee1JQ)
licence: n/a (no code release found); paper CC BY 4.0
implement_or_borrow: (1) Page-function mapping: only expose actions valid on the current route -> directly reduces action hallucination; (2) explicit navigate(url) tool whose enum is the deep-link map; (3) send action metadata once at page load, push observations lazily only when URL or UI changes (cheap context); (4) session-scoped state {latest observations, page-filtered function set, last n chat turns, executed actions}; (5) separate web-interaction agent from analysis agent (MCP tools for analytics) and chat summariser; (6) test harness: replay a recorded frontend observation over the socket, assert the exact function call + params or target URL - reuse as the team's intent-to-destination / UI-state correctness test.

hybrid_evidence: Design is hybrid by construction (GUI primitives + composite functions + MCP analytics) but no comparison numbers.
small_model_evidence: None (Llama 4 Maverick only; authors state any competent instruction-tuned LLM can be used).

title: WebMCP (W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group Draft Community Group Report)
venue: W3C Community Group Draft Report (not a W3C Standard, not on Standards Track); version dated 8 October 2026
core_idea: A browser API letting a web page register JavaScript 'tools' (name, description, JSON inputSchema, execute callback, annotations) that a browser-integrated or external AI agent can discover and invoke, instead of actuating the UI. Editors from Microsoft (Brandon Walderman) and Google (Khushal Sagar, Dominic Farolino); test suite at wpt.fyi/results/webmcp.
headline_results: Spec, no performance numbers. IDL (current draft): document.modelContext (SecureContext) with registerTool(ModelContextTool, {exposedTo, signal}), getTools({fromOrigins}), executeTool(RegisteredTool, inputObject, {signal}) and events toolchange / toolactivated / toolcancel. ModelContextTool = {name, title, description, inputSchema, execute(inputObject, {signal}), annotations}. ToolAnnotations = {readOnlyHint, untrustedContentHint, consequentialHint, debugging}. Security section covers tool poisoning, output injection, misrepresentation of intent, over-parameterization privacy leakage; mitigations incl. Permissions Policy disable, max input lengths, untrusted/consequential annotations. Note: entry point is document.modelContext in the current draft; earlier explainers and many blogs use navigator.modelContext (third-party sources report a rename - not verified against browser release notes).
verification: verified-fulltext (official spec HTML fetched 2026-10-09 and IDL index read); browser shipping status (Chrome origin trial, Edge flag) seen only in secondary blogs - unverified
licence: spec under W3C Community Contributor License Agreement; GitHub API license=NOASSERTION ('Other')
implement_or_borrow: Shape window.__vacp action descriptors to be WebMCP-compatible so the same registry can later be published via document.modelContext.registerTool: {name, title, description, inputSchema (JSON Schema), annotations {readOnlyHint, consequentialHint, untrustedContentHint}}. Use consequentialHint (or equivalent) to trigger the human-confirmation gate before state-changing ERP actions; readOnlyHint for data reads; emit a 'toolchange'-like event when the capability set changes on navigation; support AbortSignal-style cancellation.
risks: Draft CG report, API surface has changed (navigator -> document.modelContext per current draft); not available in all browsers; local vLLM agent would need its own bridge anyway (e.g., Playwright page.evaluate) - so implement window.__vacp first and treat WebMCP as an export format. Security papers show tool-surface injection risks (see 2606.06387, 2608.24017).
small_model_evidence: None. No arXiv paper found that benchmarks WebMCP task success vs DOM/vision agents; only security-focused arXiv papers (2606.06387, 2608.24017) evaluate WebMCP.
arxiv_id_title_check: no arXiv ID (checked via official page)

title: Build the web for agents, not agents for the web
core_idea: Position paper introducing the Agentic Web Interface (AWI): an interface designed for agents rather than forcing agents through human UIs, DOM trees, screenshots or raw APIs. Proposes six principles (Standardized, Human-centric, Safe, Optimal representations, Efficient to host, Developer-friendly) and concrete suggestions: unified higher-level actions, UI-compatible bidirectional AWI<->UI state, agent access control with explicit confirmation for destructive actions, progressive information transfer, agentic task queues.
headline_results: No experiments (position paper).
implement_or_borrow: Use as design checklist for window.__vacp: 'optimal representations' (agent can request exactly the info type/granularity -> scoped getState/getCapabilities), 'compatibility with user interfaces' (every agent action must be reflected in the visible UI state the human sees - same store), 'access control for agents' (ACL per action + explicit user confirmation for destructive actions), 'human-centric' (user can pause/steer mid-trajectory).
risks: No empirical evidence; venue not confirmed.
small_model_evidence: None.

title: ActionEngine: From Reactive to Programmatic Web Agents via State Machine Memory
core_idea: An offline Crawling Agent builds a state-machine graph (SMG) of the web app: GUI states, operations available in each state (navigation, update, data-access with output schemas) and transitions. At runtime an Execution Agent synthesises a complete program in one planning call and executes it deterministically, with a reactive fallback that repairs failures and patches the SMG.
headline_results: WebArena, 655 tasks across 4 domains, all methods on Claude Opus 4.6: ActionEngine 91.2% success vs Claude Code (with Playwright MCP) 82.7% and AgentOccam 56.8%. Shopping Admin +21.1 pts over Claude Code; Reddit 95.0% vs 92.4%; GitLab tie at 89.0%. Average latency 27 s vs Claude Code 87 s (3.2x) and AgentOccam 787 s (29x). Input tokens reduced 14-22x vs Claude Code; LLM calls 1.5-3.5 per task vs 7-16 for reactive baselines; cost $0.05/task vs $0.40 (Claude Code) and $0.34 (AgentOccam). Crawler-only SMG: 73.1%; online refinement +18.1 pts average. Crawl cost $11.6-$37.2, 36-260 min; break-even 39-101 tasks.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v2: abstract, Section 5 results, appendix)
implement_or_borrow: For the API agent and for a VACP bridge: the app already knows its own state machine, so hand-author (instead of crawl) a page/state graph with operations per state and output schemas; let the 32B reasoning model emit one complete plan over named operations (single planning call), execute deterministically, and only re-plan on a structured failure -> fewer LLM calls and lower latency on vLLM. Include data-access operations with output schemas (bind results to variables).
risks: Single frontier backbone (Claude Opus 4.6); remaining failures from ambiguous intent (~23 cases) and search-dependent tasks (~22); plan-then-execute cannot adapt to unseen results; authors note weaker planners may need the sketch-repair safety net.
hybrid_evidence: Programmatic execution with reactive (Playwright) fallback outperformed pure reactive agents on success, latency and cost.
small_model_evidence: None (Claude Opus 4.6 only).

title: AutoWebWorld: Synthesizing Infinite Verifiable Web Environments via Finite State Machines
core_idea: Model a website as an explicit FSM (states, actions with preconditions and effect rules, goal states), have coding agents generate the front-end from the FSM, BFS-enumerate goal-reaching trajectories and keep only those that replay successfully in Playwright. Because transitions are explicit, step correctness and task success are verified programmatically, producing cheap verified training data for GUI agents.
headline_results: 29 environments, 11,663 verified trajectories at $0.04 per trajectory. Ours-7B (Qwen2.5-VL-7B trained with GRPO on ~16K synthesized steps) WebVoyager overall 27.42% (15-step limit) vs UI-TARS-1.5-7B 26.51% and Qwen2.5-VL-7B 5.62%; Ours-3B 15.09%. ScreenSpot-Pro: 3B 13.3->18.0, 7B 23.2->27.5; ScreenSpot-v2 7B 84.83->86.16.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v1, method and results sections)
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the evaluation idea, not the training: write the ERP app's pages/filters as an explicit FSM (state = route + filter/date/sort values; actions with preconditions and effects), then (a) validate every agent execute() call against preconditions (action-hallucination = call not legal in current state), (b) auto-generate test utterances + gold end states by BFS over the FSM for UI-state correctness and multi-step success KPIs.
risks: Targets GUI-agent training, not declared interfaces; synthetic sites; absolute WebVoyager numbers are low.
small_model_evidence: 3B/7B Qwen2.5-VL models gain from verified synthetic data (numbers above) - GUI grounding, not tool calling.

title: Where Did It Go Wrong? Process-Level Evaluation of Web Agents with Semantic State Tracking (WebStep)
core_idea: WebStep: 10 self-hosted websites and 1,800 tasks where each site's GUI is rendered from a deterministic semantic MDP (state = interface position s^p such as URL/search/filter/pagination/modals + revealed item attributes s^i; typed semantic actions). The environment logs the semantic trajectory in the background, enabling process metrics (exploration SR, execution SR, information coverage, GUI/semantic step ratio) and bifurcation analysis of the decisive error.
headline_results: Table 2 (Terminal SR / Exploration SR / Execution SR / Info coverage % / GUI steps / Semantic steps / GUI:Semantic): Fara-7B 35.7/47.3/75.0/76.4/18.9/8.3/2.3; GUI-Owl-1.5-8B 34.4/43.3/78.6/79.5/28.3/10.4/2.7; UI-TARS-1.5-7B 37.1/49.2/73.9/80.3/35.0/14.0/2.5; Qwen3.5-122B 58.2/66.3/86.7/89.1/22.1/9.8/2.3; OpenAI CUA (GPT-5.4) 82.7/89.4/92.4/96.8/19.7/10.0/2.0; Claude CUA (Sonnet 4.6) 85.3/91.0/93.7/96.3/14.3/9.3/1.5. On Q&A, Claude CUA beats OpenAI CUA by 30% on navigation actions but trails by 6.7% on inspection.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v2: Section 2 MDP definition, Table 2)
implement_or_borrow: Make the app's semantic state (the same store behind window.__vacp.getState) the source of truth and log every transition: then compute, per run, exploration correctness (did the agent reach the right page/filters), execution correctness, and the GUI-to-semantic step ratio - directly maps to the team's intent-to-destination, UI-state correctness and steps KPIs, and lets you compare API agent vs VACP agent on the same trace format.
risks: Evaluates GUI agents only (no declared-interface agent); synthetic sites.
small_model_evidence: 7-8B GUI agents cluster at 34-37% terminal SR vs 82-85% for frontier CUAs on GUI operation.

title: CI4A: Semantic Component Interfaces for Agents Empowering Web Automation
core_idea: Instrument a UI component library (23 Ant Design component categories) so every mounted component registers a semantic triplet <State view S, Tool signatures T, Metadata M> in a global registry window.__ci4a__ offering getStatus() (state, tool signatures with typed/enum/required constraints, metadata) and callTool() (deterministic business-logic execution via the component's own event handlers). A hybrid agent (Eous) dynamically extends its action space with the tools of components on the current page and falls back to low-level actions.
headline_results: Refactored WebArena (Ant Design, 182 tasks; a11y-tree depth 12.1->16.2), all GPT-5: Eous (vision mode) 86.3% SR vs AgentOccam 70.3% and Seed-1.8 end-to-end 61.5%; Eous (structured mode) 75.3% vs WebArenaBase 26.4% and AgentOccam text-only 69.2%. Average steps reduced from 10.7 to 4.5 in text (Table 1 caption says 4.7). Long tasks: baselines 37.15% vs Eous 51.4% (structured) / 74.3% (vision). Cascader component: 1.1 vs 4.2 steps, accuracy 74%->100%.
code_url: Anonymous GitHub link in paper (no public repo confirmed)
implement_or_borrow: Closest prior art to a component-level window.__vacp for a no-code app: register each widget (filter, date picker, grid, chart) on mount/unmount with its own state view and tool signatures, tag the DOM node with a stable id (data-cid), and route callTool() through the widget's normal change handlers so the UI and agent stay in sync. Include enum ranges and required flags in tool signatures to fix 'constraint invisibility' (e.g., valid date range, allowed filter values).
risks: Requires intrusive instrumentation of the component library; evaluated on a refactored WebArena subset with GPT-5 only; minor inconsistency in reported average steps (4.5 vs 4.7).
hybrid_evidence: Best result (86.3%) is the vision+semantic hybrid (SoM screenshot + semantic triplets) vs 75.3% for a11y-tree+semantic triplets.
small_model_evidence: None (GPT-5 only).

title: Building the Web for Agents: A Declarative Framework for Agent-Web Interaction (VOIX)
venue: arXiv preprint; a version titled 'VOIX: A Web-Native Interface for Agents' appears in Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Web Engineering (DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-29372-5_15, per Crossref)
core_idea: Sites declare agent capabilities directly in HTML with <tool> (name, description, parameters, optional return) and <context> (task-relevant state) elements; a browser extension reads them, prepends contexts to the conversation, sends available tools to the user's chosen inference provider, and dispatches tool calls as events to the page's handlers. Evaluated for learnability in a 3-day hackathon with 16 developers.
headline_results: Latency benchmark (GPT-5-mini; seconds; VOIX vs Perplexity Comet vs BrowserGym): Creative Studio add triangle 2.32 vs 27.21 vs 25.29; rotate triangle 1.11 vs 89.12 vs Failed; delete 0.96 vs 16.29 vs 5.69; export 1.30 vs 10.12 vs 4.25; Fitness week plan 14.38 vs 229.52 vs 1271.00; start day 1 1.07 vs Failed vs 26.27; Project mgmt create task 1.62 vs 26.14 vs 33.01; copy task 2.67 vs 61.94 vs Failed. 16 participants built 6 apps.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v1, incl. latency table); LNCS version verified via Crossref metadata only
implement_or_borrow: Declarative fallback for window.__vacp: render <context> blocks for the current page state (active filters, date range, sort) and <tool> elements per action so state and actions are co-located with the component that owns them; use a 'return' flag so the agent waits for the tool result before replying. Their limitation note is directly useful: atomic GUI-mirroring tools give little gain; intent-level tools give large gains but must be designed carefully.
risks: Latency comparison is per-task single measurements vs very different systems (Comet, BrowserGym) on the authors' own apps; no success-rate benchmark; developer-burden of keeping tools in sync with GUI.
small_model_evidence: GPT-5-mini used for the latency benchmark; no open small-model results.

title: MCP vs RAG vs NLWeb vs HTML: A Comparison of the Effectiveness and Efficiency of Different Agent Interfaces to the Web (Technical Report)
venue: arXiv preprint (OpenAlex also lists ACM DOI 10.1145/3774904.3792893; venue not confirmed)
core_idea: Controlled testbed of four simulated e-shops, each exposed via HTML, MCP (per-shop Web APIs) and NLWeb (natural-language query -> schema.org JSON), plus a RAG agent over crawled content; identical tasks (search, price comparison, substitutes/complements, checkout). First head-to-head comparison of interface types with the same tasks and models.
headline_results: Table 3 micro-averages (CR / F1 / tokens per task / cost / runtime): HTML 0.57 / 0.67 / 241,136 / $0.52 / 291 s; RAG 0.68 / 0.77 / 46,667 / $0.10 / 50 s; MCP 0.62 / 0.75 / 139,569 / $0.27 / 62 s; NLWeb 0.64 / 0.76 / 71,214 / $0.10 / 53 s. Best config RAG + GPT-5: F1 0.87, CR 0.79. Models: GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4. MCP/NLWeb show larger variation across models, i.e., more dependence on model capability.
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v1: abstract, Section 4 Table 3)
licence: none detected (no LICENSE file found on main; GitHub API unavailable at check time)
implement_or_borrow: Evidence for the team's API-agent vs browser comparison: structured interfaces cut tokens ~2-5x and runtime ~5x vs HTML while raising F1 ~0.08-0.10. Borrow the measurement protocol (CR, F1, tokens, cost, runtime per task, same tasks across interfaces) for the API agent vs VACP agent vs (optional) DOM baseline. Note MCP's token cost was high because each shop had its own function names/JSON format - argues for one uniform action schema across pages.
risks: E-commerce domain; simulated shops; MCP implementation per-shop heterogeneous; venue unconfirmed.
small_model_evidence: GPT-5-mini included (RAG + GPT-5-mini named as good cost/performance compromise); no open-weight models.

title: WidgetVA: A Widget-Centric Framework and Benchmark for Agentic Visual Analytics
core_idea: Standardises VA components as widgets with explicit state, action APIs (filter, zoom, highlight, navigate... instantiated per widget, e.g., line.zoomXRegion) and side-effect-free perception queries (Inspect / Summarize / Compute), plus a library of reusable analytical workflows (single- and multi-widget). WidgetVABench scores Answer, Reference-Trace similarity and final State separately across four settings: No Tools, Direct Tools, Widget Abstraction, Widget Abstraction + Workflow.
headline_results: Multi-widget tasks: moving from Direct Tools to Widget Abstraction raises Answer by 5.8 pts, Trace by 15.1 and State by 23.1 pts (averaged over models); GPT under Widget+Workflow reaches Answer 60.7% vs human reference 57.1%. Single-widget: all models best under Widget+Workflow; Widget Abstraction raises Answer for GPT and Gemini but slightly lowers it for Qwen while Qwen's Trace and State rise. Flat Direct Tools add little on multi-widget tasks (Gemini Answer slightly decreases vs No Tools). Models: GPT-5.6-Luna, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct (Claude Sonnet 4.6 used as judge).
verification: verified-fulltext (arXiv HTML v1: Sections III, V; per-cell Table II values not extracted)
licence: none detected (no LICENSE file found on main)
implement_or_borrow: Split the bridge's actions into state-changing actions vs side-effect-free perception queries (Inspect: config/raw rows; Summarize: quick aggregates; Compute: correlations/derived metrics) and mark them; expose coordination links (filter on widget A affects widget B) in getState so cross-view effects are attributable; ship a small workflow library (e.g., aggregate-to-detail, period-over-period comparison) in the planner prompt. Use the Answer / Trace / State three-way scoring for the team's analytical-faithfulness and UI-state KPIs.
risks: Very recent (Sep 2026) preprint; VA tasks on generated workspaces; LLM judge for open-ended tasks.
hybrid_evidence: Orchestrator gives the agent both the rendered view and the widget state each turn; humans relied on visual inspection while agents used perception queries for 29-41% of successful calls.
small_model_evidence: Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct (open, ~3B active) benefits in Trace/State from widget abstraction but not in Answer; evidence-to-answer errors remain more frequent for Qwen than GPT.

title: TwinBI: An Agentic Digital Twin for Efficient Augmented Interactions with Business Intelligence Dashboards
core_idea: Couples an LLM multi-agent system with an executable BI dashboard state reconstructed from a unified interaction log (chat turns, dashboard operations, tool metadata), over a Cube semantic layer (measures, dimensions, hierarchies, join paths). Exposes schema views, SQL, logs and an /insights command for state-grounded summaries so chat answers stay consistent with filters/hierarchies on screen.
headline_results: Controlled A/B, same Playwright browser agent with gpt-5-mini, 30 analytical queries (5 families incl. QoQ growth, cross-view comparison, trap tasks), 30-step budget: exact-match 43.3% -> 63.3%, partial-credit 48.3% -> 70.8%, timeout rate 40.0% -> 10.0% (Dashboard alone -> TwinBI). Usability study N=5.
licence: none detected (no LICENSE file found on main)
implement_or_borrow: Closest domain match (BI dashboard over sales data). Borrow: (1) a semantic layer (measures/dimensions/hierarchies) that both the dashboard and the agent query, so numbers in answers come from the same definitions as the widgets (faithfulness KPI); (2) a unified interaction log as the provenance record behind getState; (3) gold answers cross-checked by three paths (DB query, semantic-layer API, dashboard) - reuse for building the team's analytical-correctness test set; (4) 'trap' tasks testing filter stability and policy compliance.
risks: Small benchmark (30 queries) and usability study (N=5); baseline is UI-only agent, not an API agent.
hybrid_evidence: TwinBI = UI agent + chat/backend tools (hybrid) vs UI-only: large accuracy and timeout improvements.
small_model_evidence: gpt-5-mini backbone (small API model); no open-weight models.

title: Designing Agent-Ready Websites for AI Web Agents: A Framework for Machine Readability, Actionability, and Decision Reliability
core_idea: Framework of three dimensions (agent interpretability, agent executability, agent decision reliability) for making e-commerce sites agent-ready via machine readability, semantic clarity, action cues, evidence signals and temporal-validity indicators. Controlled experiment: human-oriented baseline vs agent-ready variant of the same site, browser agents unchanged.
headline_results: 5 tasks x 3 models (GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 4 Fast) x 300 runs: PASS 134/150 vs 74/150 (strict success 89.3% vs 49.3%); PARTIAL 43 -> 3; average steps 9.31 -> 6.49; prompt tokens down 18.72% (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 40.47% (Grok 4 Fast), 37.43% (GPT-4.1).
code_url: replication package referenced in paper (not checked)
implement_or_borrow: Cheap wins even for the DOM fallback path: explicit labels/ARIA on filters, visible current-state indicators (active filter chips, selected date range), evidence/validity signals (data as-of timestamps) - these also help the VACP state snapshot (include as-of timestamps and units).
risks: Single e-commerce prototype, 5 tasks, human-annotated PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL; still browser agents (not declared tools).
small_model_evidence: Includes smaller API models (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 4 Fast); no open-weight models.

title: WebMCP Tool Surface Poisoning: Runtime Manipulation Attacks on LLM Agents
core_idea: Identifies Mid-Session Tool Injection (MSTI): third-party scripts inject or alter WebMCP tools during an active session. Two classes: Tool Hijacking (changing the visible tool set via AbortSignal or registration races) and Tool Framing (manipulating name, description, readOnlyHint, inputSchema).
headline_results: Demonstrates both attack classes succeed against WebMCP implementations with GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 2.5-flash agents (per-condition rates in paper, not extracted here). Recommends binding tool identity to origin, lifecycle consistency, data boundaries for third-party tools, and traceable registration/invocation logs.
verification: verified-fulltext for threat model and recommendations (arXiv HTML v1); per-model attack-success numbers not extracted
implement_or_borrow: Guardrails for window.__vacp: freeze the action registry (no runtime registration from arbitrary scripts), validate that every executed action name exists in the snapshot the agent planned against (VACP's snapshot-validity check), never trust readOnly flags from untrusted code, and log every registration and invocation.
risks: Security-only; attack surface mainly relevant if the app embeds third-party scripts.
small_model_evidence: None.

title: WebMCP-Phalanx: Enforcing and Characterizing Trust Boundaries for Browser-Integrated LLM Agents
core_idea: Dual-layer runtime for WebMCP: a browser-native trust anchor binding each tool to its registering principal with cryptographically protected capability credentials and provenance labels, and a dual-LLM split where a Quarantine LLM (no tool authority) inspects tool metadata/outputs for prompt injection before a Privileged LLM executes.
headline_results: Ownership mechanism reduces revocation/overwrite attack success from 100% to 0%; dual-agent runtime blocks all 80 prompt-injection attempts in tool descriptions; 2 of 80 attacks via tool return values still succeed; no statistically significant utility loss vs no-attack baseline.
implement_or_borrow: If time permits: treat tool outputs that contain free text from ERP records as untrusted (WebMCP untrustedContentHint analogue) and keep the executing agent from acting on instructions found in data; registry ownership = only the app's own bridge module can register actions.
risks: Adds a second LLM call (latency) - likely overkill for a 48h hackathon with a first-party app.
small_model_evidence: None.

title: MCP Apps: Interactive User Interfaces for MCP (SEP-1865, MCP extension; builds on MCP-UI and OpenAI Apps SDK)
venue: Model Context Protocol Specification Enhancement Proposal (status Final per official SEP page); spec in modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps (spec version 2026-01-26 linked from README)
core_idea: Lets MCP servers declare UI resources under the ui:// scheme (initially text/html;profile=mcp-app), associate them with tools via metadata, and exchange messages bidirectionally between the embedded UI and the host over MCP JSON-RPC, so tool results can render as interactive charts/forms/dashboards inside chat clients.
headline_results: Specification, no performance numbers.
verification: verified via official SEP page summary (search result) and ext-apps README/LICENSE fetched; spec text itself not read in full
licence: ext-apps: Apache-2.0 for new contributions (MCP project transitioning from MIT; docs CC-BY-4.0); mcp-ui: Apache License 2.0 (LICENSE file)
implement_or_borrow: Relevant to the UX deliverable (render charts, summary cards and comparisons on the fly in the companion): return a structured chart spec + a ui:// resource from the analysis tool rather than prose; reuse the bidirectional message pattern so a click in the rendered card can call back into window.__vacp (e.g., 'open this page with these filters').
risks: Host support varies; designed for chat hosts (Claude/ChatGPT), not an in-app copilot - the team may only borrow the pattern.
small_model_evidence: None.
arxiv_id_title_check: no arXiv ID (checked via official page)

title: A Benchmark to Understand the Role of Knowledge Graphs on Large Language Model's Accuracy for Question Answering on Enterprise SQL Databases
core_idea: Builds an enterprise insurance SQL benchmark of 43 questions split into question-complexity x schema-complexity quadrants, plus an ontology+mappings context layer. Compares GPT-4 zero-shot text-to-SQL against text-to-SPARQL over a knowledge-graph view of the same database.
headline_results: Average Overall Execution Accuracy (AOEA), GPT-4 zero-shot: all questions SQL 16.7% vs KG/SPARQL 54.2% (abstract rounds to 16% vs 54%). Per quadrant SQL->KG: Low Q/Low S 25.5%->71.1%; High Q/Low S 37.4%->66.9%; Low Q/High S 0%->35.7%; High Q/High S 0%->38.5% (Sec 5.2 says 38.7%; inconsistency in source).
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the quadrant design: tag each of our test utterances by question complexity (single measure vs multi-measure/compare/drill) and schema complexity (#tables/joins behind the measure) and report accuracy per quadrant for raw-SQL baseline vs our named-operation layer. Reuse the ACME schema+43 questions as an external sanity check of our tool layer if time permits.
risks: Single domain, 43 questions, GPT-4 only, 2023; SPARQL not SQL, so effect mixes 'semantic context' with 'query language'. Execution accuracy ignores partially correct answers.
hybrid_evidence: Yes: KG/ontology context layer vs raw schema, same model, same questions.
small_model_evidence: None (GPT-4 only).

title: Increasing the LLM Accuracy for Question Answering: Ontologies to the Rescue!
core_idea: Adds a deterministic Ontology-based Query Check (OBQC) that validates LLM-generated SPARQL against ontology domain/range rules, and an LLM repair loop fed with the check's error explanations (max 3 cycles, else answer 'unknown'). Shows that symbolic validation + repair + abstention raises accuracy and cuts error rate on the same enterprise benchmark.
headline_results: All questions AOEA: first attempt 42.88%, with repairs 72.55%, unknown 8%, accuracy+unknown 80.56%, error rate 19.44% (abstract: 72% accuracy, 8% unknown, 20% error), vs prior 54.2% accuracy / 45.8% error. Quadrant with repairs: Low Q/High S 17.20%->76.33%; High Q/High S 28.17%->60.62%. Most-fired rules: Double Domain 37.47%, Domain Range 22.78%.
implement_or_borrow: Implement directly: a deterministic validator over every tool call (measure exists, dimension is valid for measure's grain, filter value in domain, date range valid, join path allowed) that returns machine-readable error strings to the 14B/32B model for up to 3 repair attempts, then abstains with 'I don't know' instead of guessing. Count 'unknown' separately from 'wrong' in our KPIs.
risks: Same 43-question benchmark as predecessor; GPT-4 only; ontology rules are RDFS-level only (no unions/complex OWL).
hybrid_evidence: Yes: symbolic check+LLM repair vs LLM alone; quantifies gain from deterministic validation.
small_model_evidence: None reported.

title: Semantic Layer vs. Text-to-SQL: 2026 Benchmark Update (dbt Labs)
core_idea: dbt Labs re-runs the Sequeda ACME insurance questions (11 questions x 20 runs) comparing agent text-to-SQL against querying through the dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow), on raw and on a re-modeled dbt project. Argues SL failures surface as errors/refusals while text-to-SQL failures are plausible wrong numbers.
headline_results: Modeled project: claude-sonnet-4-6 text-to-SQL 90.0% vs Semantic Layer 98.2%; gpt-5.3-codex 84.1% vs 100.0%; gpt-5.2 text-to-SQL 68%. Original unmodeled schema, All: text-to-SQL 2023 (GPT-4) 32.7%, Sonnet 4.6 64.5%, GPT-5.3 Codex 64.5%; SL 2023 60.5%, 2026 72.7%; on questions not needing too many hops SL 83.1% (2023) / 100.0% (2026) vs T2S 26.9%/62.5%/51.2%; on too-many-hops questions SL 0.0%. Reasoning-effort sweep: SL 87.2%-100.0% vs T2S 50.0%-65.0%.
verification: verified-fulltext (blog page read directly; not peer-reviewed; numbers as published by vendor)
implement_or_borrow: Copy the framing for our pitch and eval: run each test question N times (e.g., 5-10) through (a) our named-operation layer and (b) a raw text-to-SQL baseline with the same local model, report accuracy and the 'out-of-scope -> explicit error' rate. Design measures so that multi-hop questions (order->line->product->supplier) are pre-modeled, because SL coverage gaps scored 0%.
risks: Vendor with commercial interest; only 11 questions so one question moves score ~9 points; full schema in context for T2S; frontier models only.
hybrid_evidence: Yes: semantic layer vs text-to-SQL on same questions/models; also shows coverage limitation (0% on un-modeled multi-hop).
small_model_evidence: None (frontier API models only).
arxiv_id_title_check: no arXiv ID (checked via official page)

title: Semantic Layers for Reliable LLM-Powered Data Analytics: A Paired Benchmark of Accuracy and Hallucination Across Three Frontier Models
core_idea: Paired single-shot benchmark of 100 questions over the Contoso Retail dataset in ClickHouse: each model gets schema-only vs schema plus a 4 KB hand-written semantic document (measures, conventions, disambiguation rules). Finds the document, not model choice, explains essentially all significant variance.
headline_results: Adding the semantic document improves accuracy by +17 to +23 percentage points across Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4; with it models score 67.7-68.7%, without it 45.5-50.5%; every cross-cluster comparison significant at p < 0.01.
verification: verified-abstract (HTML full text returned 404; per-model numbers not checked)
implement_or_borrow: Cheap first step: write a ~4 KB semantic card for our ERP measures (definitions, grains, units, fiscal calendar, status filters like 'exclude cancelled orders') and inject it into the planner prompt; use a paired design (with/without card, same questions) as our ablation, with a paired significance test.
risks: Single-shot SQL generation (not an agent), frontier models only, single dataset; full-text details unverified.
hybrid_evidence: Yes: schema-only vs schema+semantic doc, paired, same models.
small_model_evidence: None.

title: Which Part of the Context Layer Does the Work? Separating Semantic Content from Retrieval Scaffolding in Text-to-SQL Agents
core_idea: Four-arm ablation on DABstep using a YAML 'data contract' (allowed tables, forbidden operations, 14 metrics with executable sql_expression, domain descriptions) exposed through 9 tools (list_metrics, lookup_metric, trace_metric_impacts, inspect_query, run_query, ...). Separates semantic content from the retrieval/tool scaffolding and from pre-computed views.
headline_results: Hard-task accuracy schema -> contract arm: GLM (glm-5.3-flash) 13.9% -> 55.1%; DeepSeek (deepseek-v4-flash) 22.6% -> 56.6%; Sonnet 5 22.9% -> 68.4%; GPT-5.6 37.0% -> 77.4%. Hollow (scaffolding, empty prose) arm: 19.3/22.6/38.0/51.2%; manual (knowledge pasted in prompt) arm: 22.9/42.9/23.8/50.3%. Contract SQL carries fee semantics up to 98% vs 4% for prompt arm. Ungoverned arms submitted 166 mutating statements; governed arms none. Compiled views: gold on all 176 covered tasks.
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the tool surface almost verbatim for our semantic layer: list_metrics / lookup_metric / lookup_relationships / trace_metric_impacts (= our 'related') / inspect_query-then-run. Keep metric definitions in one YAML that both tools and validator read. Takeaway for 14B/32B: put semantics behind a lookup tool rather than a long prompt; pre-compute views only where the model fails.
risks: Single-author; one benchmark domain (payments fees); models are API-served (fp8 'flash' variants); gains confined to the contract's domain.
hybrid_evidence: Strong: isolates semantic content vs tool scaffolding vs prompt-pasted knowledge vs compiled views.
small_model_evidence: Partial: two cheaper 'flash' models (GLM, DeepSeek) gain most (13.9->55.1, 22.6->56.6) but sizes not stated; no 7-32B local model.

title: GROUND: Reducing Hallucinations in LLM-Based Enterprise Analytics Through Governed Semantic Definitions
core_idea: Constrains LLM analytics to a governed semantic layer: binds intent to approved metrics/dimensions and validates generated SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, row-level-security and cost rules before execution, retrying (up to 3 revisions) or abstaining. Compared with direct text-to-SQL, schema-RAG and semantic-only grounding under one model.
headline_results: Synthetic 100-question benchmark (Claude Opus 4.8): result (value) accuracy Direct 0.000, Schema-RAG 0.000, Semantic-only 0.500, GROUND 0.951; any-hallucination rate 0.79 / 0.54 / 0.40 / 0.00. Real NHTSA data, 40 questions, independent gold: result (value) 0.65 / 0.62 / 0.68 / 1.00; any-hallucination 0.78 / 0.68 / 0.33 / 0.00. Enforced guarantees hold with zero violations on every model (incl. Llama-3.3-70B).
implement_or_borrow: Implement the validator taxonomy as our hallucination metric: per answer, flag schema/metric/join/grain/filter/security violations and report 'any-hallucination rate' (target 0). Grain check (COUNT DISTINCT order_id vs line fanout) is directly relevant to order/order-line ERP tables.
risks: Single author; synthetic benchmark built by the same author; judgment behaviours (refusing undefined metrics) still fallible; no licence on repo.
hybrid_evidence: Yes: direct vs schema-RAG vs semantic-only vs governed semantic layer, same model.
small_model_evidence: Llama-3.3-70B tested only on adversarial set for guarantee holding; no 7-32B.

title: Business Truth, not SQL Accuracy: A Rule-Gated 7B Analytics Agent Outperforms a Direct-Prompted 32B Baseline
core_idea: Introduces WarehouseReliabilityBench (400 tasks, two synthetic warehouses, ~half of correct responses are clarify/abstain/refuse) and QueryProof, a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B agent whose behaviour is set by rules derived from a semantic layer and catalog and whose answers are gated by deterministic post-execution checks (required filters/period applied, non-empty, no impossible values). Scores 'Business Truth Rate' where correct abstention counts as correct.
headline_results: 80-task test split: BTR QueryProof base 0.562, routed 0.537 vs 32B direct 0.300, 7B retrieval 0.300, 7B few-shot 0.275, 7B direct 0.100; paired difference vs 32B +0.237 [+0.112, +0.375]; 71.0% lower cost per correct answer. False success rate 0.754 (32B direct) -> 0.351; 0 wrong numbers on answerable tasks (0 of 24). Resampling template families widens intervals to include zero.
verification: verified-fulltext (headline table; models = Qwen2.5-Coder family, run locally quantised)
implement_or_borrow: Most directly transferable: copy BTR + False Success Rate as KPIs, include ~30-50% clarify/abstain/refuse items in our test set, and add post-execution assertions on every tool result (filters/period applied, non-empty, sane value ranges e.g. no negative inventory, margin within [-100%,100%]). Evidence that scaffolding lets a small model beat a bigger unscaffolded one.
risks: Single author, synthetic warehouses, 80-task test evaluated once; compares systems not model sizes; no component ablation; effect magnitude uncertain.
hybrid_evidence: Yes: rule-gated semantic-layer agent vs direct/few-shot/retrieval baselines.
small_model_evidence: Strong: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B scaffolded (BTR 0.562) beats Qwen2.5-Coder-32B direct (0.300), local quantised.

title: Never the Number: Structural Abstention for AI Systems Whose Answers Are Consumed as Fact
core_idea: Proposes a 'trusted kernel, generative shell' pattern: the LLM may only influence which question is answered, never which value is returned; a deterministic kernel maps fully specified questions to a bounded set of answerable shapes and compiles them to queries. The user confirms the interpreted question before any value is computed, and unrepresentable requests are declined.
headline_results: No quantitative results: comments state it 'contains no code, schemas, datasets, or performance metrics'; reports a two-year production case study qualitatively.
implement_or_borrow: Adopt the invariant as our design rule: the 14B/32B model emits a structured operation spec (measure, dims, filters, period); the backend computes numbers; the UI shows the interpreted spec (confirmation card) before state-changing actions; narrative text may only cite numbers returned by tools (enforce by checking every number in the answer against tool outputs).
risks: Position/architecture paper, no metrics; cannot cite for accuracy gains.
small_model_evidence: None.

title: Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows
core_idea: 632 enterprise text-to-SQL workflow problems over BigQuery/Snowflake/local DBs with schemas often >1,000 columns, requiring metadata/doc search and multi-query workflows. Establishes that raw enterprise text-to-SQL remains far from reliable even for frontier agents.
headline_results: Spider-Agent + o1-preview solves 21.3% (vs 91.2% Spider 1.0, 73.0% BIRD). Table 5 (Spider 2.0): Qwen2.5-72B 6.17%, DeepSeek-V2.5 5.22%, Llama-3.1-405B 2.21%, o1-preview 21.36%. Table 3: Spider 2.0-lite/snow DeepSeek-V3 8.78%/8.78%, Qwen2.5-Coder 5.30%/5.48%, o1-preview 23.22%/23.77%.
implement_or_borrow: Cite as justification for NOT letting the local model write free-form SQL: open models score ~5-9% on enterprise SQL. No need to run it in 48h.
risks: Different task (free SQL over huge schemas) than our bounded operation catalogue; open-model numbers from late 2024.
hybrid_evidence: Indirect: shows raw text-to-SQL weakness, no semantic-layer arm.
small_model_evidence: Open models 2.21%-8.78%; Qwen2.5-Coder (size per table) 5.30% lite.

title: BEAVER: An Enterprise Benchmark for Text-to-SQL
core_idea: Enterprise text-to-SQL benchmark from private data warehouses: 9128 question-SQL pairs from real query logs over 812 tables in 19 domains, with synthesized expert-verified queries isolating domain knowledge vs query complexity. Adds annotations for five subtasks enabling fine-grained diagnosis.
headline_results: SOTA agentic frameworks with GPT-5.2 achieve only 10.8% accuracy; with all subtask annotations as oracle hints accuracy rises to 30.1%.
licence: not verified (repo not resolved; GitHub API rate-limited)
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the 'oracle hint' ablation: measure our agent's accuracy when given gold intent slots (page, measure, filters) vs predicted, to separate intent-resolution errors from execution/analysis errors.
risks: Abstract-only verification; results are for frontier model; domain knowledge is the bottleneck, which a semantic layer addresses only if modeled.
hybrid_evidence: Indirect: oracle subtask hints (proxy for domain knowledge) roughly triple accuracy 10.8%->30.1%.
small_model_evidence: Not checked.

title: BIRD-INTERACT: Re-imagining Text-to-SQL Evaluation for Large Language Models via Lens of Dynamic Interactions
core_idea: Multi-turn text-to-SQL benchmark coupling each DB with a hierarchical knowledge base (DAG of facts, ambiguity created by masking nodes), metadata and a function-driven user simulator; tasks cover full CRUD for BI/operational use with ambiguous and follow-up sub-tasks. Evaluates a protocol setting (c-Interact) and an open agentic setting (a-Interact).
headline_results: GPT-5 completes 8.67% of tasks in c-Interact and 17.00% in a-Interact (follow-up SR). Table 2 (Full): Qwen-3-Coder-480B c-Interact priority/follow-up 22.00/10.83, a-Interact 13.33/4.17; Deepseek-Chat-V3.1 18.50/8.50 and 17.17/4.83; Claude-Sonnet-4 a-Interact 27.83/12.67.
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the function-driven user simulator pattern (classify agent's clarification question into AMB/LOC/UNA, answer from annotation) to test our agent's clarify-before-act behaviour on ambiguous utterances like 'show me last quarter's slow movers' without a human.
risks: Free SQL incl. writes; no small open models evaluated; heavy setup.
small_model_evidence: None at 7-32B (only 480B Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek V3.1).

title: InsightBench: Evaluating Business Analytics Agents Through Multi-Step Insight Generation
core_idea: 100 business datasets (e.g., finance, incident management) with planted insights; agents must pose questions, analyse, and summarise insights and actions end-to-end. Proposes AgentPoirot baseline and a two-way evaluation with LLaMA-3-70B as open-source judge, matching each ground-truth insight to its best-scoring predicted insight.
headline_results: Table 1 (5 seeds), insight-level LLaMA-3-Eval: AgentPoirot gpt-4o 0.60+-0.03 vs Pandas Agent gpt-4o 0.54+-0.01; gpt-4-turbo 0.56; gpt-3.5-turbo 0.50; llama-3-70b 0.52+-0.04; generic goal drops gpt-4o to 0.40. Summary-level LLaMA-3-Eval: gpt-4o 0.44 vs PA 0.40.
implement_or_borrow: Copy the planted-insight methodology into our synthetic ERP tenant: inject known causes (e.g., one supplier's late deliveries -> stockouts -> revenue dip in one region/month) and score whether the agent's 'likely causes' recover them, using best-match per planted insight with a local judge (Qwen2.5-14B) plus exact checks on the cited numbers.
risks: Open-ended LLM-judge scores are soft (0.5-0.6 range, small gaps); free pandas code generation, not tool calls; only open backbone is Llama-3-70B.
small_model_evidence: Llama-3-70B backbone 0.52 insight score vs gpt-4o 0.60; no 7-32B.

title: DABstep: Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning
core_idea: 450+ real tasks from a financial (payments) analytics platform requiring code-based processing plus reasoning over heterogeneous documentation, with factoid answers checked automatically (numeric tolerance, order-insensitive lists, fuzzy string match). Hard split exposes multi-step reasoning failures.
headline_results: Best agent 14.55% on hard tasks (o4-mini; easy 76.39%). Table 1: Deepseek R1 hard 11.04/easy 68.21; Llama 3.3 70B 3.70/68.06; Llama 4 Scout 1.85/52.78; Llama 3.2 1B 0.00/1.39; GPT-4o 6.08/66.67.
licence: Dataset CC BY 4.0 (per paper); code licence not stated
implement_or_borrow: Copy the scorer: factoid answers with numeric tolerance (paper is inconsistent between 1e-2 and 1e-4; pick and document one), order-insensitive list compare, normalised string match. Use it for our 'number-trace' test items so analytical correctness is scored without an LLM judge.
risks: Domain is payments fees, not ERP; free-code agents; easy split nearly saturated.
hybrid_evidence: No (but 2609.22259 shows a data-contract layer lifts DABstep hard accuracy several-fold).
small_model_evidence: Llama 3.3 70B hard 3.70%; no Qwen 7-32B.

title: DAComp: Benchmarking Data Agents across the Full Data Intelligence Lifecycle
core_idea: 210 enterprise tasks: data-engineering (multi-stage SQL pipelines) scored by execution, and open-ended data-analysis tasks scored by an LLM judge guided by hierarchical rubrics (multiple valid solution paths; completeness, accuracy, insightfulness) plus Good-Same-Bad comparison against baseline reports. Validated judge-human agreement.
headline_results: Abstract: DE success under 20%, DA averages below 40%. Table 5 DA score (DA-Agent): GPT-5 50.84, DeepSeek-V3.1 34.33, Qwen3-Coder 25.13, Qwen3-235B-A22B 13.25, Qwen3-8B 4.47. Table 3 DE: GPT-5 43.45, Qwen3-8B 19.89. Judge (Gemini-2.5-Flash) vs humans: rubric item kappa_w 0.834, case ICC 0.890 (human-human 0.906 / 0.925). (Text leaderboard Table 8 gives different DA values, e.g. GPT-5 56.14; inconsistency in source.)
licence: not verified (repo not resolved; GitHub API rate-limited)
implement_or_borrow: Copy the hierarchical rubric with alternative solution paths for our open-ended 'why did X drop' questions (e.g., path A: supplier delay; path B: price change), with weighted items for completeness/accuracy/insight; validate the local judge on ~30 items against a human rater and report kappa.
risks: LLM-judge dependence; rubric authoring is costly; table/text inconsistencies.
small_model_evidence: Qwen3-8B DA 4.47 vs GPT-5 50.84: small open models very weak on open-ended analysis without structure.

title: BI-Agent and BI-Bench: Towards Automating End-to-End Business Intelligence
core_idea: BI-Bench: 100 test cases of (question, answer) pairs extracted from real public BI dashboards (Power BI/Tableau projects), requiring table search, transforms and joins. BI-Agent decomposes BI into tool calls (search, join, transform) and is post-trained (SFT+RL) on synthesized trajectories.
headline_results: Frontier LLMs <50% accuracy. Table 3 SQL vanilla->tools: o4-mini 48.2->61.9; GPT-5.5 46.7->60.2; GPT-OSS-120B 5.3->45.3; Qwen3-8B 5.2->19.8. Post-trained Qwen3-8B RL-Tool 35.0 (SQL). NL2SQL systems: Kwai-AutoSQL-32B 17.3, XiYanSQL-QwenCoder-32B 7.7, Kwai-AutoSQL-14B 7.8. Scoring: table match with np.isclose rtol 1e-2, atol 0.5, permutation-invariant, 10 runs.
implement_or_borrow: Borrow the tolerant table-equality scorer (shape + cell match, permutation-invariant, numeric tolerance) for comparing our tool outputs to gold. Evidence for tools > free SQL for small models: Qwen3-8B 5.2 -> 19.8 with tools.
risks: Dashboards are public hobby/enterprise projects; no Qwen2.5-14B/32B general models; repo has no licence.
hybrid_evidence: Yes (tool-augmented decomposition vs vanilla SQL/Python, same models).
small_model_evidence: Qwen3-8B 5.2->19.8 (tools), 35.0 after RL; 14B/32B NL2SQL specialists 7.7-17.3.

title: Structured Composition of Verifiable Atomic Insights for Table-to-Report Generation
core_idea: ComInsight enumerates 'atomic insights' from parameterised SQL templates (MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM, COUNT, GROUP_BY, CORR, TREND) filtered by significance and an LLM interestingness judge, links them in an insight graph (logical/temporal/hierarchical edges), and composes higher-order conclusions. Every output carries executable SQL and provenance.
headline_results: InsightBench (gpt-5.5 backbone): I-Eval 0.73+-0.03 vs AgentPoirot 0.60+-0.03; S-Eval 0.55 vs 0.44; I-ROUGE-1 0.42 vs 0.32. T2R-Bench average 83.5% vs 64.61% (GPT-5.5).
implement_or_borrow: Implement a mini version for 'likely causes': enumerate atomic facts via our analyze() over each candidate dimension (supplier, region, product, channel) for the two periods, keep statistically notable deltas, and let the LLM only compose/explain them, citing atom ids. Gives faithfulness by construction.
risks: Very recent (Oct 2026), no code; backbone is gpt-5.5 (judge is fine-tuned Llama-3-8B); reported baseline labelling inconsistencies.
small_model_evidence: Uses fine-tuned Llama-3-8B only as interestingness judge.

title: Business Utility of Large Language Models as Exploratory Data Analysis Agents
core_idea: Root-cause-style EDA benchmark on an agent-based supply-chain simulation: agents must identify supplier-product combinations responsible for low quality and downstream sales loss from indirect operational traces. Scores with Jaccard vs deterministic ground truth, coefficient of variation over 5 trajectories, and a risk-adjusted 'Business utility'.
headline_results: 15 model-variant configurations from 8 families; GPT-5.4 (extra-high reasoning) best: experiment-averaged mean score 0.8748, Business utility 0.6952; most configurations not reliable enough for autonomous EDA.
implement_or_borrow: Copy for our 'likely causes' KPI: plant a supplier x product cause in synthetic ERP data, score Jaccard of the agent's cause set vs planted set, run 5 repeats per question and report mean and CV (repeatability) - cheap and LLM-judge-free.
risks: Abstract-only; simulation domain; open-model results not checked.
small_model_evidence: Not checked (abstract does not name small models).
